info.title: retnd /api/v1
info.summary: The authoritative definition of the versioned /api/v1 boundary.
info.description: Issue #166 (B6.2). This document, not the Go handlers and not the TypeScript client, is the definition of /api/v1. Both sides are generated from it (scripts/api/generate.sh) and both are held to it by a drift check (scripts/api/check-contract-drift.sh plus the conformance tests named in docs/api/contract.md). Compatibility and deprecation rules are in docs/api/contract.md.

servers.description: Every path in this document is relative to the versioned base path. /health/live and /health/ready are deliberately NOT in this contract: they sit outside /api/v1, carry no authentication and exist for an orchestrator, not for a client of this API.

session.name: retnd_session
session.description: The authenticated session. For the generic runtime profile this is apps/common/auth/local's own HTTP-only cookie; a runtime profile with a native gateway (native_auth) establishes the same session from provider identity headers accepted only from a trusted peer. Which mechanism established it is a profile concern; that a caller of a secured operation has one is not. This cookie has had two earlier names, one per rename of this project: bm_session before #794 renamed it to backupd, and backupd_session before EPIC R (#885) renamed the product to retnd. The runtime still ACCEPTS both names on a read, for one release, so an in-place upgrade does not sign every caller out; it issues only the name declared here, and a request arriving under a deprecated name has that same session re-issued under this one on that read, so the old name leaves the wire on the caller's next request. A client should carry back whatever the runtime set. Both windows close in the same release, the one after the release that renames this product.

csrf.name: X-CSRF-Token
csrf.description: The double-submit CSRF token (apps/common/csrf). Required on every operation this API serves with a mutating verb, with no exception: that includes test-connection and host-key-probe, whose effect is read-only but which each open an outbound connection to a caller-supplied host, and a request that reaches the network is exactly what a cross-site form must not be able to make. It is never a value an operator configures or a client is issued out of band. The runtime mints it, delivers it in the retnd_csrf cookie below, and a caller echoes that value back here unchanged; a generator that renders this as a user-supplied API key has read it wrongly. Whether an operation needs it is stated twice, in that operation's own security block and in its x-csrf-required, and scripts/api/check-contract-drift.sh fails when the two disagree.

csrfCookie.name: retnd_csrf
csrfCookie.description: The other half of the double-submit pair above, and the half a client has to READ. The runtime issues this cookie on any response that does not already carry one, and a caller echoes its value back in X-CSRF-Token; the two are compared byte for byte. It is declared here because a client cannot implement the csrf requirement from this document without knowing which cookie to echo, and until it was, the only place that name existed was the two implementations. This cookie has had two earlier names, one per rename of this project: bm_csrf before #794 renamed it to backupd, and backupd_csrf before EPIC R (#885) renamed the product to retnd. For one release the runtime accepts any of the three names on a read, and a request arriving with only a deprecated one has that same token re-issued under the name declared here rather than being given a second, different one - so a client that echoes the value it found under either name is accepted, and a client written against this document reads the current name and finds it.

bootstrapToken.name: X-Bootstrap-Token
bootstrapToken.description: The single-use enrollment secret printed to the runtime's own log. Only /auth/enroll accepts it.

IdempotencyKey.name: Idempotency-Key
IdempotencyKey.description: Caller-supplied key that makes a retried submission a replay rather than a second operation. Reusing one key for two different operation bodies is IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_CONFLICT, never a silent second run.

ApiErrorCode.description: Every error code this API contract knows. `wire` codes are the machine-readable tokens a server may put on the wire; `ui` codes are the shared web UI's own presentation vocabulary, which no endpoint ever emits and which is listed here so there is exactly one registry rather than a second hand-maintained copy in ui/shared. A code is registered here once, whatever number of operations emit it: NOT_CONFIGURED is emitted by every operation an unconfigured instance refuses, and is declared on each of them. `unknown` is the sentinel an unrecognised code off the network degrades to.

ConnectionCheck.description: One step of a connection test. `outcome` is passed, failed or skipped, and skipped is a first-class answer rather than a quiet pass: a surface that renders a skipped authentication as anything but "this was never tried" has told an operator their credentials are fine on the strength of a step that never ran. `category` is the machine-readable half a surface branches on; `detail` is a sentence the engine composed and never an underlying transport error's text. This is MediumPreflightCheck's shape asked about a SOURCE instead of a destination, deliberately, so a preflight table and a connection-test table are two renderings of one idea rather than two contracts.

step.description: What this step proves. `credentials` is whether the key this backup set names can be resolved and used on THIS host at all: the reference resolves to a key this deployment holds, and the file's own mode and its whole containing directory chain are still what a real transfer demands. Nothing about the far side, and nothing that opens the private half. `resolve` is whether the hostname resolves, and to what, because "it resolves" and "it resolves to the machine you think" are different claims and only an operator can settle the second. `connect` is whether TCP to host:port answered, and what identification string came back, which is how you know you reached sshd and not a load balancer. `host_key` is which key the server offered and whether the known_hosts this set verifies against actually trusts it for this host: the comparison is knownhosts' own, the same one the transport will make, never a second opinion that could be wrong in the permissive direction. `authenticate` is whether the server accepted that key for that user, and it is skipped when the host key did not match, because offering a credential to a server whose identity has not been established is the thing FR-6 exists to prevent. `list` is the configured remote path listed over the real transport, and how many entries came back; it is the only step that proves the path in the configuration is a path on that machine. `write_probe` is whether these credentials may WRITE and REMOVE under that path, proven by creating a uniquely named probe file there and deleting it again; it is the only step that changes anything on the far side, it runs last because nothing may be written to a path the `list` step has not established, and it is the one step whose `no` is not a failure: a read-only source backs up perfectly and simply cannot be deleted from, which is what `writable` reports and what a delete-from-source control is enabled on.

outcome.description: `skipped` is a real answer and not a quiet pass: it means an earlier step failed in a way that makes this one meaningless, and `detail` says which. A surface that renders a skipped authenticate as anything but "this was never tried" has told an operator their key is authorised on the strength of a step that never ran.

category.description: The category a failure classified as, absent when the step passed or was skipped. It is the machine-readable half: a client branches on this and never on `detail`.

detail.description: What this step found, in words, for a person to act on. Always present, including on a skipped step, where it is the reason nothing was tried.

duration_ms.description: How long this step took on its own, in milliseconds. Present only on the steps that are measured separately: credentials, resolve, connect and host_key. Absent on authenticate and list, which are decided from ONE call and have no timing of their own, and absent rather than zero, because a 0 ms beside a green step reads as "instant" when what it means is "never measured".

TrustedHostKey.description: ONE host key a backup set actually pins, named the way an operator compares it: the algorithm and the SHA256 fingerprint, the form `ssh-keygen -lf` prints and the wizard's verify step shows. Never the key material, which is a wall of base64 nobody checks by eye.

algorithm.description: The host key algorithm, as an SSH implementation names it ("ssh-ed25519", "ssh-rsa", "ecdsa-sha2-nistp256"). Read off the key itself, never assumed: a panel that printed a fixed algorithm beside a fingerprint told an operator with an RSA anchor that they had trusted an ed25519 one.

fingerprint.description: The SHA256 fingerprint, "SHA256:" prefix included, byte for byte what `ssh-keygen -lf` prints for the same key. It is the whole of what an operator has to compare against the host.

VersionResponse.description: GET /system/version. Nothing here names an implementation: no rclone, no SQLite, no filesystem path.

engine_version.description: The transfer engine's own version string, deliberately not named after the engine.

config_revision.description: The optimistic-concurrency token a client echoes back on POST /operations. Read here rather than scraped out of a 409's prose.

deployment_id.description: Which deployment this is, as opposed to what it currently holds. Minted once per instance and stable across every configuration edit, so two instances built from the same template are told apart by it where a config_revision, being a hash of configuration content, reports them as the same. A client about to send a mutation compares it against the deployment the command was aimed at, so a write typed at one instance with another instance's address configured is refused rather than carried out somewhere nobody was looking. Empty on an instance that cannot name itself, which a client reads as unconfirmable rather than as agreement.

ready.description: True once the runtime has completed its startup sequence.

configured.description: False on an instance listening with no configuration at all: it is serving the first-run setup flow, not the application, and every operation outside that flow refuses with 503 NOT_CONFIGURED. A different question from ready above, and both answers matter separately: an unconfigured instance is never ready, but a not-ready instance is not necessarily unconfigured. GET /system/first-run asks this and nothing else, for a client that does not already fetch this response.

adopted_paths.description: Which of this deployment's locations, if any, are being served from a pre-rename path. Empty on every deployment whose paths are the ones this release resolves, which is the normal case. A non-empty entry means the renamed path holds nothing and the pre-rename one holds the data, so the pre-rename one is what is live: this is the third of the three surfaces that report that (the others are `retnd check` and the startup log), and it is the one a client or a support transcript can read without a shell on the host. Each entry is reported rather than warned about because the warning is printed once per start and an operator asks the question months later.

AdoptedPath.description: One of this deployment's locations that is being served from a pre-rename path, and the renamed path it would otherwise have used. A location is adopted only when the renamed path holds nothing and the pre-rename path holds the data; two populated locations that are different directories make the runtime refuse to start instead, and are therefore never reported here.

what.description: Which location this is, in the words the runtime uses for it: "configuration" or "state database". The two are resolved by different code and are reported separately, because a deployment can have adopted one and not the other.

serving.description: The absolute path actually in use: the pre-rename one.

renamed.description: The absolute path this release resolves, which holds nothing. This is the path an operator's compose file and persisted configuration should be moved to.

CapabilitiesResponse.description: GET /system/capabilities. The API expression of the PlatformCapabilities contract (apps/common/platform/capabilities). A capability says what a platform CAN do; it never says who MAY do it, and server-side authorization never consults it.

platform.description: The runtime profile's stable platform identifier.

local_path.description: The configured destination directory for this set, as the operator entered it.

free_bytes.description: Observability only. level is decided from available_bytes.

ManagerStorage.description: The one manager-wide storage reading: what the backup root's filesystem holds, what this manager itself accounts for, and which of the two the gauge is a fraction of. Distinct from the per-backup-set list beside it, which answers a different question and cannot answer this one: a fresh instance has no backup sets, two sets on one volume are two entries reporting the same disk, and the storage cap is one ceiling for the whole manager. When known is false every byte count is 0 and level is empty; render that as "capacity is not known yet", never as zero bytes and never as a percentage.

known.description: False means no reading could be taken. Every numeric field below is then 0 and must not be displayed as a measurement.

unknown_reason.description: Why known is false. no_backup_root: this configuration cannot say which filesystem to measure (no backup sets yet, or sets on different volumes). not_created: the backup root is known and does not exist yet, which is normal before the first cycle. unreadable: it exists and could not be read, which needs a person. misconfigured: the capacity numbers cannot produce a verdict, or a cap is set and this manager's own usage could not be measured.

measured_path.description: The directory whose filesystem was statted, reported whether or not the reading succeeded. The engine runs in a container and the reading must be of the backup root as the container sees it; naming the path is what makes a reading of the wrong mount noticeable.

free_bytes.description: Every free block, including any only a privileged process could allocate into. Observability only.

available_bytes.description: Free space this process may actually use (df's Avail). This, not free_bytes, is what level and every refusal are decided from.

catalog_bytes.description: How much space this manager is occupying, summed from the sizes the state database records for artifacts whose local copy the journal says exists. This manager's own consumption, not the volume's.

catalog_bytes_known.description: Separates "we summed the catalog and it came to zero", which is correct on a deployment that has transferred nothing, from "we could not read the catalog".

other_bytes.description: How much of what the filesystem reports as used this manager does NOT account for. Surfaced rather than hidden: a large gap means something else is writing into the backup root.

cap_bytes.description: The configured ceiling on how much space this manager may use. 0 means no cap, never a zero-byte ceiling.

denominator.description: What limit_bytes is. "disk" is the whole filesystem, which is what a deployment with no cap is measured against; "cap" is the operator's allowance. A bar at 80% of a 2 TB disk and one at 80% of a 100 GB cap are different facts and must not render identically.

limit_bytes.description: The denominator in effect: the cap when one is set, otherwise the filesystem's total.

used_bytes.description: The numerator: this manager's own consumption when a cap is set, otherwise how full the volume is (total minus free).

headroom_bytes.description: How much room is left before the binding constraint refuses a transfer: the smaller of available_bytes and the cap's remaining allowance.

binding_constraint.description: Which constraint produced headroom_bytes, which is a different fact from denominator: a capped deployment whose volume is nearly full is bound by the disk, and an operator watching their allowance has no reason to expect that. Empty when known is false.

warning_free_bytes.description: The configured warning level, weighed against headroom_bytes. 0 means no warning level.

critical_free_bytes.description: The configured critical floor, weighed against headroom_bytes. 0 means no critical level.

level.description: Empty when known is false. An unread disk is not OK.

ListStorageStatusResponse.description: GET /system/storage. The manager-wide reading a dashboard gauge is drawn from, plus one entry per configured backup set.

SubmitOperationRequest.description: POST /operations. The idempotency key is a header, not a body field: it is a property of the retry, not of the operation. action selects which of the parameter objects below is read; restore_placement reads restore, run_backup_set reads backup_set_id, restore_snapshot reads snapshot_restore, verify_snapshot reads snapshot_verify, hold_snapshot reads snapshot_hold, release_snapshot_hold reads snapshot_hold_release, and run_cycle reads none of them. A body naming another action's parameters is refused rather than ignored: a server that ignores fields it did not expect teaches clients those fields are optional, and the next reader of that client cannot tell which operation was meant. Every mutating incremental-backup action this product has is on this one route, which is what makes each of them durable, idempotency-keyed and revision-checked without a second answer to how long work begins.

action.description: What to submit. An enumerated action name, never a command line.

config_revision.description: Optimistic concurrency: the revision the caller believes is current. A stale value is refused with CONFIG_REVISION_STALE and nothing runs.

backup_set_id.description: The one backup set a run_backup_set acts on, as the source/backup-set id every surface in this product prints. Absent for run_cycle, which is deployment-wide, and refused when a run_cycle carries one: a body naming another action's parameters is a request that has confused two operations.

snapshot_restore.description: Read by restore_snapshot and refused for any other action.

snapshot_verify.description: Read by verify_snapshot and refused for any other action.

snapshot_hold.description: Read by hold_snapshot and refused for any other action.

snapshot_hold_release.description: Read by release_snapshot_hold and refused for any other action.

skip_workflow_scripts.description: Take the backup and run NONE of this backup set's workflow hook scripts. run_backup_set's parameter, and refused when any other action carries it, exactly as backup_set_id is. It exists for one situation and is shaped for it: a hook is broken at three in the morning and somebody needs tonight's backup. Three things keep it from being taken by habit. It is an ADMINISTRATOR action, and on this API the administrator boundary is the destructive gate this route already sits behind -- a deployment that has not turned destructive operations on cannot submit one at all, and the refusal it gets is DESTRUCTIVE_OPERATIONS_DISABLED. A scheduled run can never carry it, which is not a rule this route enforces because no schedule submits through it. And a backup set with an unresolved workflow interruption refuses the run outright, before the flag is even looked at, because that set may have a machine sitting quiesced and skipping the cleanup is the last thing anybody should do to it. Every bypassed run is recorded twice: on the durable operation row, so a bypass that was asked for and refused is still visible, and as a warn-level event naming the actor. This field is a plain boolean, so `false` is indistinguishable from absent and is accepted by any action: what refuseForeignParameters refuses is an action other than run_backup_set that CARRIES IT AS TRUE, which is the only spelling that asks for anything.

Operation.description: One durable operation record. Timestamp fields are omitted, not zero-valued, until the event they name has happened. progress is the separate, ephemeral thing: see OperationProgress for why it is a nested object that is simply absent rather than a set of fields on this record.

cycle.description: The counts a finished run cycle recorded, absent for every other operation and for one that has not finished. Absent is not a row of zeroes: a cycle that is still running has not walked nothing, it has not finished walking.

snapshots.description: The snapshot runs this operation performed, absent for every operation that performed none. Present here rather than only under the backup set because an operation is what a client polled: a surface that submitted a run and then had to guess which of the set's snapshots belonged to it would attribute the wrong one every time two runs overlapped.

OperationProgress.description: Live progress for an operation that is running in THIS process right now (docs/EPIC-B-multi-nas.md §52). It is sampled from the transfer engine while a run cycle executes and is never written to the operations table: an operation record is durable and crash-safe, and progress is neither, so persisting it would put a tick-rate write path on the one record whose durability guarantees exist to avoid exactly that, and would resurrect a dead cycle's last reading after a restart as though it were live. So this field is present only while the cycle producing it is executing here. A finished operation, and one that was running before a restart, both carry no progress object at all, which is not the same answer as zero and must not be rendered as one. Nothing here is a percentage of the whole operation: a run cycle is a pass over every enabled backup set, and the artifacts it will find are not known when it starts, so no honest denominator for the whole exists. The byte counters describe the ONE artifact being copied at observed_at; the counters beside them say where in the cycle that artifact sits.

RetentionTierSelection.description: One tier's claim on an artifact, and which of the two placements made it. FR-18 places every artifact twice, once by the timestamp this manager discovered it and once by the producer's own timestamp on the remote object, and KEEP is the union. FR-8 treats the second as untrusted, so which pass selected a tier is a different fact with different consequences and travels with the tier rather than with the verdict: one artifact can be selected by DAILY through one placement and by MONTHLY through the other.

tier.description: A configured tier name upper-cased, or the reserved LAST_KNOWN_GOOD. The value set is OPEN: the retention chain is operator-defined, so SEMI_ANNUAL or any other name a config file spells arrives here.

selected_by.description: DISCOVERY when only the discovery placement selected this artifact for this tier, PRODUCER when only the producer's own timestamp did, BOTH when both did. PROTECTION is not a placement at all: it is FR-19's last-known-good term, which is not a bucket selection and so names neither timestamp.

RetentionVerdict.description: What the plan decided for one artifact, and why.

medium.description: Where the copy this verdict is about lives, when that is a configured storage medium (EPIC E, FR-30). ABSENT means the implicit local medium, which is where every copy in a deployment that declares no storage medium is; spelling local by absence is what keeps such a deployment's response exactly what it was before this field existed, and the command-line dry-run states the same asymmetry the same way. It is also absent on the two REFUSE verdicts that establish nothing at all, a location the journal records twice (a move in flight) and a backup whose local path could not be resolved; each says so in its own reason, and a kept one is additionally named in the plan's unconfirmed_placements. A DELETE always establishes its medium, so on a deletion absent means local and nothing else, which is the question FR-30 asks this field to answer: "delete 40 backups" means something very different when half of them are objects in a bucket somebody else pays for.

tiers.description: Which tiers kept this artifact, in the order the configured chain lists them. Empty for a DELETE or REFUSE verdict. tier_selections lists the same tiers in the same order and says which placement selected each; read that one to answer why an artifact was kept.

tier_selections.description: The same tiers as `tiers`, in the same order, each paired with the placement that selected it. Empty for a DELETE or REFUSE verdict.

RetentionMove.description: One backup this plan would relocate, and both ends of the move (EPIC E, FR-27). A move is a statement about PLACEMENT and nothing else: planning one never adds a backup to the keep set and never removes one, which is why moves travel beside the verdicts rather than inside them. There is deliberately no field here for what a provider would charge to run this, how long a provider might take, or the key material that reaches either end, and there never will be: this product holds none of those three, so a field for one could only be filled with a guess.

artifact.description: The backup's own name, not its fully-qualified id. A plan is already scoped to one backup set, so re-spelling the set on every row would be noise a client has to strip to render a table.

from_medium.description: Where the one confirmed copy is today: "local" for the backup set's own directory on this machine, or the id of a configured storage medium, spelled exactly as Placement.medium spells it.

to_medium.description: The medium the first tier in chain order that selects this backup names as its home. Always different from from_medium: a backup already at home is not a move.

RetentionPlan.description: A server-computed retention plan. The client may only apply one by id; it never proposes what to delete.

inventory_revision.description: Optimistic concurrency, half one: the inventory this plan was computed against.

config_revision.description: Optimistic concurrency, half two: the configuration this plan was computed against. Either moving makes the plan stale and the apply is refused.

operation_id.description: Set on apply, absent on preview.

moves.description: Every backup this plan would relocate, in verdict order (EPIC E, FR-27). Absent in a deployment that declares no storage medium, which is every deployment before EPIC E. It travels with the plan rather than behind a second call because an apply is confirmed against a plan_id, and what that plan_id commits to has to be the whole of what was shown: a moves section fetched separately could be rendered beside verdicts it does not belong to.

unconfirmed_placements.description: Every kept backup whose current location could not be established, in verdict order: the journal holds no confirmed copy of it, or holds more than one, which is a move already in flight. No move is planned for one, and that is exactly why the list exists rather than the backup being quietly skipped: "I could not confirm where this is" and "this is already where it belongs" produce the same silence and are not the same claim. Absent in a deployment that declares no storage medium, where there is nowhere else a copy could be and the answer would be noise on every backup an upgrade inherits.

retention_is_override.description: Whether this plan was computed under the backup set's own retention policy rather than the deployment's. 'Why is this artifact being deleted' has a different answer, and a different fix, depending on which one was in force.

plan_id.description: The plan the operator approved. A plan the server no longer recognises, or one computed against a moved revision, is refused.

CreateBackupSetRequest.description: POST /backup-sets. The backup-set spec, plus the two things only a create can ask for: that the new set also runs at once, and that it may take over history already on its id.

allOf.description: The create-only additions on top of the spec itself.

run_immediately.description: Also submit a run_cycle. This branch, and only this branch, is subject to the destructive gate.

acknowledge_repoint.description: Confirm creating this backup set somewhere other than where the history already on its id came from. Removing a backup set frees its id up, and a set created over an id that already has artifacts on record takes every one of them, so creating it at a different host, remote_path or local_path is the same move an edit makes. Needed only when this id has artifacts on record AND one of those three differs from what is recorded for them; re-creating a set exactly where it was removed from asks nothing. It is not a field of the backup set and nothing persists it: it answers one refusal, for one request.

BackupSet.description: A persisted backup set as the API reports it.

stable_for_seconds.description: The window the "stable" completion strategy waits for, and 0 for every other strategy. Served so an edit surface offering the strategy can offer the window with it: selecting "stable" without one is a configuration this service refuses. Whole seconds, truncated rather than refused: a configuration is only required to make stable_for positive, so a stable_for of 1500ms loads and is served here as 1, and any window under a second is served as 0, which this field already spends on "not the stable strategy". A client cannot tell those two apart. The write path refuses a sub-second window instead of rounding it, on the grounds that a value meaning one thing over this wire and another in the file is a divergence both routes report as success; the read path does not, so a set configured with a sub-second window reads back here as a different set from the one that was written. Read it as the budget rounded down, never as the budget.

stale_after_seconds.description: How long this backup set may go without a fresh backup before it is reported as stale (FR-24's freshness budget). BackupSetSpec has always accepted it on the way in and UpdateBackupSetRequest has always been able to change it, so until now this was a field the API could write and could not read back, and a client that changed it had no way to show what it had changed it to. Zero is how an engine built before this field answers, and a client reads it as not reported rather than as a set with no freshness budget. It cannot mean a configured budget of none: a configuration that leaves stale_after unset or non-positive is one this service refuses to load. It can mean a budget under a second, because the value is truncated to whole seconds on the way out while nothing refuses sub-second precision on the way in, so `stale_after: 1500ms` is served as 1 and `stale_after: 500ms` as 0.

retention_is_override.description: Whether this backup set declares its own retention policy rather than being retained under the deployment's (issue #333). The policy itself is not here: read it from /backup-sets/{source}/{set}/retention, which serves the resolved chain, the deployment's chain beside it, and the raw override. A list of sets needs the attribution, not three numbers that only fit one shape of chain.

trusted_host_keys.description: Every host key this backup set's known_hosts actually pins for this set's own address, read from that file rather than restated from the configuration, because the file is what a connection checks. A LIST because a host legitimately answers with more than one key algorithm and OpenSSH writes a line for each, so a set pinning both an ed25519 and an RSA key is in ordinary shape and reporting one of them would show an operator a fingerprint the server in front of them may not present. ABSENT is "this deployment could not report what this set trusts", and it is what a local-transport set, an unreadable anchor and a file pinning nothing for this address all produce; a client must say that rather than render a blank where a fingerprint goes. An engine built before this field answers the same way, so a client cannot read absence as "this set trusts nothing".

trusted_host_key_recorded_at.description: When THIS deployment last wrote the trust anchor above. Absent when the backup set points at a known_hosts file this deployment did not write: a file an operator maintains by hand is usually shared with other sets, so its timestamp is about whatever was last added to it rather than about this set's host, and reporting it would answer "when was this host key trusted" with something else.

ssh_key_id.description: The key-store id this set's key resolves to, the same value POST /ssh-keys returned and GET /ssh-keys lists. The id only: what it resolves to is a server-side path and this API never publishes one. Never omitted, and EMPTY IS A REAL ANSWER, meaning this set uses a key this deployment does not manage, which is every set pointing at a mounted or hand-provisioned key file. It is here because BackupSetPatch has always been able to WRITE ssh_key_id and nothing could read it back, so a surface offering to replace a set's key could not name the key being replaced.

connection_unverified.description: Whether this backup set was written without its SSH connection ever having been proven (issue #624). True means a surface deliberately skipped a check it could have run, which is `backup-set create --no-verify` and nothing else; a connection test that PASSES against the set clears it, and one that fails leaves it alone. ABSENT is not "unverified": every configuration written before this field existed says nothing, an engine built before it answers nothing, and a client that read silence as a mark would declare every backup set on every deployment unproven on the first upgrade. Read absence as "nothing here says this was skipped".

poll_interval_seconds.description: This backup set's own poll-interval override, or NULL when it inherits the deployment default. Null is a real answer: a form must not put the deployment's number in the box, because saving it would pin this set to today's default and detach it from one it was tracking.

effective_poll_interval_seconds.description: How often this backup set is actually polled: its own override, or the deployment default when it has none. Resolved by the engine so no client combines the two scopes itself.

engine.description: Which machinery produces this backup set's restore points: "artifact" or "kopia". Always reported, and always the RESOLVED value: a configuration that omits the key reads "artifact" here rather than empty, because a client that had to know the default would be a second place the default is decided.

uuid.description: The durable identifier the snapshot lineage hangs off. Empty for an artifact set, which has none.

repository_domain.description: The repository security boundary this set's snapshots are stored in. Empty for an artifact set.

source_consistency.description: The resolved consistency mode. Empty for an artifact set: resolving it for an engine that reads it nowhere would report a claim nobody made.

verification_level.description: The resolved verification level. Empty for an artifact set.

verification_sample_percent.description: The sample size a content_sample verification reads, 0 for a set that configures none.

verification_full_every_seconds.description: The full-content-read cadence in whole seconds, 0 for never.

verification_restore_drill_every_seconds.description: The restore-drill cadence in whole seconds, 0 for never.

source_mount_prefix.description: The declared mount prefix, empty when the whole remote path is the source's own.

CreateBackupSetResponse.description: POST /backup-sets. The created set, plus at most one of operation (the run_immediately branch started) or run_error (it did not). Always 201: the set itself exists either way.

allOf.description: The create-only additions on top of the backup set itself.

ListBackupSetsResponse.description: GET /backup-sets. An object with one array field, never a bare top-level array.

ImportSSHKeyFromCandidateRequest.description: POST /ssh-keys/from-candidate. Selecting a key this host already found is a different act from pasting one this host has never seen, and it carries a different body: an opaque handle and no key material at all. It is a separate operation rather than a second mode of POST /ssh-keys because a shared body with two optional halves would have had to stop requiring private_key_pem, and this contract does not withdraw a requirement it has already made.

candidate_id.description: Select a key GET /ssh/key-candidates already listed. This is the mode a brand new operator uses, because a default install already put a key on the machine and there is nothing for them to paste. The private half is read once, server-side, through the same validation a paste goes through, and the original is left where it is. It is an opaque handle, never a path, and it resolves only against a fresh scan of the same closed set of locations, so a path, a traversal and an id for a file outside those locations all fail the same way.

ImportSSHKeyRequest.description: POST /ssh-keys. Sent once; the caller discards its own copy immediately. Pasted material only: selecting a key this host already holds is POST /ssh-keys/from-candidate, which takes a handle instead.

private_key_pem.description: Private key material. Write-only: it is never echoed back by any operation in this contract.

passphrase.description: The passphrase that decrypts private_key_pem, when it is passphrase-protected. Optional: omit it, or send an empty string, for a key that is not encrypted, which is every request this field predates. Checked against private_key_pem at import time, so a wrong passphrase is refused here rather than discovered the first time a cycle tries to connect. Write-only, for the same reason private_key_pem is.

ImportSSHKeyResponse.description: The reference a later create-backup-set call carries instead of key material.

HostKeyProbeRequest.description: POST /ssh/host-key-probe. Opens a real outbound connection, trusts nothing.

HostKeyProbeResponse.description: What the server actually saw. Presenting it to an operator for approval is the caller's job.

TestConnectionRequest.description: POST /backup-sets/test-connection. A reachability and authentication check, in one of two modes: name backup_set_id to re-check a set that already exists, or supply the connection details to check a candidate before it is saved. Exactly one mode per request. A client testing a persisted set neither knows nor has to echo back that set's key reference and trusted host line, which is what keeps a read-only "does this still work" check from being able to test something else.

backup_set_id.description: The two-part "source/set" identity of an already-persisted backup set. When present, every other field must be absent: the connection details come from the configuration.

TestConnectionResponse.description: The outcome of a connection test, as a verdict and as the steps that produced it. `ok` and `message` mean exactly what they have always meant, so a client reading only those keeps working; `checks` is what the test actually DID, one entry per step and always all of them, in the order they run; `writable` is whether these credentials may write to the source at all. Both modes of this endpoint answer the same steps: a caller no longer has to remember which request it sent to know what shape comes back.

checks.description: One entry per step, always all of them, in the order they run: credentials, resolve, connect, host_key, authenticate, list, write_probe. Both the persisted mode (`backup_set_id`) and the candidate mode (host, user and key) populate it, so there is one breakdown here and not one per mode.

writable.description: Whether the `write_probe` step completed a real write-and-remove round trip under the remote path: a file created at a name nothing else can produce, deleted again, and its absence confirmed. It is what a client enables or disables its "delete from source after backup" control on, and what the server refuses a create, an edit or a read-only:false on when it is false. Independent of `ok`: a read-only source is a perfectly OK connection that simply cannot be deleted from, which is a supported posture and never a failure. False whenever nothing was proven, including a check that stopped at an earlier step, because nothing may enable a delete on an absence of evidence.

Validator.description: One registered application validator. An id and a sentence, and deliberately nothing else: the script it resolves to is server-side and a client never learns it.

ListValidatorsResponse.description: GET /validators. Read-only by design: a client-extensible catalog would be an arbitrary-command surface.

RetentionTier.description: One link in the retention chain, on the wire. The same shape is read and written, so a client round-trips exactly what it was served. That round trip is why every field a tier can carry is here: a chain write REPLACES the whole chain, so a field this shape omits is a field the save deletes from the operator's configuration file.

medium.description: The storage medium this tier's artifacts live on (FR-27); absent means the local backup root, which is what every chain written before storage mediums existed means. Carried on the wire so a chain write does not delete it.

RetentionSettings.description: The retention policy actually in effect. tiers is always the RESOLVED chain.

protect_last_known_good.description: Turning this off widens what a later retention apply may delete. The apply itself stays behind the destructive gate.

CapacitySettings.description: FR-21's capacity configuration as it is actually deciding. Every number is BYTES: the MB/GB picker beside the field is display only and converts at the edge, so nothing on this boundary carries a unit.

cap_bytes.description: The ceiling on how much space this manager may use. 0 means no cap: use the whole volume and report the reading against it. A sentinel, never a zero-byte ceiling, and never resolved to a number. A negative value is refused.

warning_free_bytes.description: The level at which a reading is reported as WARNING, measured against whatever headroom binds. 0 means no warning level.

critical_free_bytes.description: The floor at or below which a transfer is refused, measured against whatever headroom binds. 0 means no critical level. Must not exceed warning_free_bytes.

safety_margin_bytes.description: Held back on top of every incoming artifact's own size before a transfer is admitted.

backup_root.description: The directory whose filesystem the manager-wide reading is taken from, already resolved: the configured value when there is one, otherwise the directory every backup set's destination has in common. Empty means this configuration cannot say, which a form renders as "not known yet".

backup_root_configured.description: Whether backup_root was named by an operator rather than derived. A form must not put a derived value in an input box: saving it would pin today's derivation into the file.

ServiceSettings.description: How this manager behaves, as opposed to what it keeps: the service-behaviour settings.

poll_interval_seconds.description: The deployment-wide DEFAULT cadence a backup source is checked for new backup files at. A backup set may override it for itself (BackupSet.poll_interval_seconds), so this is not a claim about any particular set. At least min_poll_interval_seconds.

RetentionSchema.description: The closed value sets and bounds a retention chain is validated against, served rather than transcribed into a frontend.

SettingsSchema.description: The schema half of the settings response.

ServiceSchema.description: The rules the service-behaviour settings are validated against, served so a form does not keep its own copy of a bound the engine enforces.

min_poll_interval_seconds.description: The floor under BOTH scopes of the poll interval: the deployment default and any per-set override. A shorter interval is refused, wherever it was written.

SettingsResponse.description: GET and PATCH /settings both return this: the settings now in effect plus the rules they were validated against.

mediums.description: Every storage medium this configuration declares, in declaration order. Empty for a configuration that declares none, which is every configuration written before storage mediums existed.

UpdateRetentionSettings.description: A PARTIAL retention update. An omitted field is left exactly as the running configuration has it; omitting tiers leaves the chain, and a legacy file's own spelling of it, untouched.

UpdateCapacitySettings.description: A PARTIAL capacity update. An omitted field is left exactly as the running configuration has it. An explicit 0 is a request, not an omission: on this block zero means "no cap" and "no warning line", which is why every field is nullable rather than a plain number.

UpdateServiceSettings.description: A PARTIAL service-behaviour update. An omitted field is left exactly as the running configuration has it.

UpdateSettingsRequest.description: PATCH /settings. An enumerated request type, never a configuration passthrough.

acknowledge_medium_disclosure.description: The operator's acknowledgment of the storage-medium disclosure (SettingsSchema.storage.medium_disclosure). Required on, and only on, a write that FIRST sends a retention tier's artifacts to a non-local medium: without it that write is refused with MEDIUM_DISCLOSURE_REQUIRED. It is not a setting, so a request carrying nothing but this acknowledgment still names no setting to change and is refused as such.

CredentialsRequest.description: POST /auth/login and POST /auth/enroll. camelCase, unlike every schema above: apps/common/auth/local predates the snake_case convention the rest of /api/v1 uses. Recorded here as it is rather than silently normalised; see docs/api/contract.md for why fixing it is a separate issue.

SmtpSettings.description: One SMTP submission endpoint an operator typed in: where to connect, how the connection is protected, who to authenticate as, and what address the mail is from. camelCase like the rest of /auth. `password` is writeOnly and appears in NO response schema anywhere in this contract: the runtime stores it as an opaque reference to a mode-0600 file of its own and reports only whether one is set (SmtpSettingsView.passwordSet). On an update, an absent or empty `password` means "keep the stored one", which is what lets a port or a from-address be corrected by somebody who does not have the provider's API key in front of them.

security.description: How the connection is protected. `starttls` is plaintext upgraded before authentication, which is what every hosted provider documents for port 587, SMTP2go and Gmail included; `tls` is TLS from the first byte, conventionally port 465; `none` is plaintext throughout and is only reasonable for a relay on the same host or the same private network - the runtime will not send a password over it to anything but a loopback server.

SmtpSettingsView.description: SmtpSettings as a READ answers it: every field except the password, plus `passwordSet`. The password is absent structurally rather than blanked, so this shape has no field for a buggy handler to serialise material into.

passwordSet.description: Whether an SMTP password is stored at all. The whole of what this API will say about it: enough for a settings form to offer "leave blank to keep the stored password" honestly, and nothing a caller could use to learn the value.

EnrollRequest.description: POST /auth/enroll. The credentials, plus the two things issue #830 makes part of creating the administrator: the address account recovery mails to, and the SMTP endpoint it goes out over. Both are required, because an administrator with no proven way to reach its owner is an account that is permanently lost the first time a password is forgotten, and enrollment is the last moment at which somebody who can still sign in is present to fix the mail configuration. The runtime SENDS a confirmation message to `recoveryEmail` over `smtp` before it writes anything, and refuses the whole enrollment with SMTP_SEND_FAILED if that send does not succeed - leaving the single-use enrollment token unspent, so the same link can be used again once the configuration is fixed.

recoveryEmail.description: Where a forgotten-password reset link is sent. An ADDITIONAL identity field rather than a replacement for `username`, which remains the login identity: this address is used for recovery and notification only. Validated as a bare RFC 5322 address, without a display name, and refused with INVALID_EMAIL otherwise.

ForgotPasswordRequest.description: POST /auth/forgot-password. One field, and the answer never varies with it: that operation answers 204 for an unenrolled deployment, for a username that is not the administrator's, for an administrator with no recovery address, and for an SMTP endpoint that refused the message alike. It answers BEFORE any mail is attempted, so the response time does not vary either.

ResetPasswordRequest.description: POST /auth/reset-password: the token out of the emailed link, and the password to set. The token is single-use and expires; redeeming it revokes every live session and issues no new one, so whoever set the password proves they know it by signing in with it.

VerifyEmailRequest.description: POST /auth/verify-email: the token out of the emailed verification link, and nothing else. The token names the account by itself, so there is deliberately no username or address field - one would be a second thing to check and a way to ask whether an address is the administrator's. The token is single-use and expires; redeeming it makes a provisional administrator permanent.

RecoverySettingsResponse.description: GET /auth/recovery and PATCH /auth/recovery: the recovery address, the two proofs about it, the deadline an unverified one lapses at, and the SMTP endpoint without its password. `smtp` is ABSENT on a deployment whose administrator was provisioned headlessly (`auth create-admin` leaves recovery optional), which is a state a settings page has to report rather than hide - absent rather than null, the same optional-member convention every other response in this contract uses for a fact that does not exist yet.

recoveryEmailConfirmed.description: Whether a confirmation message to this address has been accepted by the operator's own SMTP server. False after the address is changed until its own confirmation send succeeds: an address nothing has ever been delivered to is not a recovery path, and reporting it as one is the silent lockout this whole feature exists to prevent.

recoveryEmailVerified.description: Whether somebody has actually OPENED the verification link that message carried (#830 s8). Separate from recoveryEmailConfirmed because the two prove different things: a mail server accepting a message proves the endpoint works and nothing more, since a typo that lands in the neighbouring domain is accepted just as happily as the right address, while a redeemed link proves the operator can READ what was sent - which is the whole of what account recovery depends on.

verificationDeadline.description: RFC3339 instant after which an administrator whose recovery address is still unverified is DELETED and enrollment reopens (#830 s9). ABSENT when this record cannot lapse - a verified address, or an administrator provisioned with no SMTP endpoint at all, which was never mailed a link to open. It is computed once, when the account is created, as max(enrollment-link window end, created_at + 30 minutes), and no later request moves it.

RecoverySettingsUpdate.description: PATCH /auth/recovery. `currentPassword` is required on every call, and at least one of `recoveryEmail`/`smtp` has to be named: a request may change the recovery address, the SMTP endpoint, or both. A changed address is re-verified by sending a confirmation over the endpoint this same request establishes, and a changed SMTP endpoint is proven the same way, with the whole update refused with SMTP_SEND_FAILED if that send fails - so a settings page cannot leave the account with a recovery address nothing has ever been delivered to, nor claim a confirmed address over an endpoint nothing has ever been delivered through.

currentPassword.description: The signed-in administrator's CURRENT password, re-checked before anything is resolved, sent or written, exactly as POST /auth/password re-checks it (and refused the same way: 401 UNAUTHENTICATED). The recovery address and the SMTP endpoint are credential-equivalent - whoever controls them controls where a reset link is delivered - so a live session alone must not be enough to repoint them, or a stolen cookie escalates into a permanent account takeover through forgot-password.

RotatePasswordRequest.description: POST /auth/password. Requires an already-authenticated session AND the current password: holding a cookie is not enough.

ErrorBody.description: The nested error body every operation outside /auth returns. code is stable and machine-readable; message is human-readable and MAY change without notice.

ErrorResponse.description: The error envelope every operation outside /auth returns. The correlation id travels in the X-Correlation-Id response header.

ConfigRevisionStaleResponse.description: The CONFIG_REVISION_STALE 409 body. It carries the current revision as a structured field so a client retries against a value it can rely on rather than one parsed out of prose.

WorkflowRefusedScript.description: One hook script that refused a workflow configuration write, and why. Only the BLOCKING half is here -- a parse error, or the error-severity findings -- because a refusal that also listed the warnings would read as though they had refused it.

dir.description: The stage directory as it is CONFIGURED rather than as it resolves, because that is the string the operator typed and the one they will recognise.

scope.description: Whose configuration declares the stage this script is in.

phase.description: Which side of the backup that stage runs on.

parse_error.description: The parser's message when the script is not a shell program at all, empty otherwise.

parse_error_line.description: The 1-based line the parser stopped at.

parse_error_col.description: The 1-based column the parser stopped at.

findings.description: The error-severity findings that refused the save, each with its position.

backup_set_id.description: The set whose stage this is, empty for a deployment-wide one. It is here because of what a ROOT change does: a deployment-wide write that moves workflows.root re-resolves every set's stage directories underneath the new root, so the write verifies those too, and a refusal naming a directory without saying whose set it is would send an operator through every backup set they have.

WorkflowScriptRejectedResponse.description: The WORKFLOW_SCRIPT_REJECTED 409 body. It carries the blocking scripts and their findings as structured fields, for the reason CONFIG_REVISION_STALE carries the current revision as one: a client that had to parse a position out of the message would be parsing prose this contract explicitly does not promise to keep stable. The message says the same thing in one string, for a terminal.

blocking_scripts.description: Every script that refused this write, in stage order then by name, so two attempts at the same save produce the same body.

AuthErrorResponse.description: The FLAT error body the /auth operations return, with the correlation id in the body as well as the header. Deliberately recorded as a second shape rather than pretended away: apps/common/auth/local diverged from the envelope above before this contract existed.

BackupSetSpec.description: Everything it takes to DESCRIBE one backup set: where it reads from, where it writes to, how it decides a file is complete, and whether it starts enabled. ssh_key_id and known_hosts_line carry REFERENCES produced by /ssh-keys and /ssh/host-key-probe, never key material. Nothing here asks for anything to be RUN, which is what makes it the body of two different operations: POST /backup-sets folds a set into a configuration that already exists, and POST /system/first-run writes the first configuration there has ever been. Those two share this base rather than restating it, so the wizard that collects these answers can never be right about one operation and wrong about the other.

validator_id.description: A registered validator's id from GET /validators. Never a path, never a command.

read_only.description: Declares this backup set's remote source read-only from creation (issue #282): pull backups from here, but never delete the remote original. Omitted or false means exactly what every request meant before this field existed.

skip_connection_check.description: Writes this set without proving its connection first (issue #624). The service runs the same six-step check POST /backup-sets/test-connection answers, in front of the write, and refuses with BACKUP_SET_CONNECTION_NOT_PROVEN when it fails; this is the deliberate opt-out, and a set written under it is marked connection_unverified until a test passes. The mark is the service's own record of the skip and is never taken from the request. Omitted or false checks, which is what every create should do.

engine.description: Which machinery produces this backup set's restore points: "artifact" (the file-at-a-time pipeline every configuration written before EPIC K uses) or "kopia" (the incremental engine, which snapshots a source TREE into a deduplicating repository). Omitted means artifact, which is what every configuration written before this key existed says. An unrecognised value is refused rather than defaulted in either direction: reading a typo as artifact silently ignores an operator who asked for snapshots, and reading it as incremental silently changes what a run does to a source tree.

uuid.description: This backup set's DURABLE identifier: the one thing about it that no rename changes. Required for an incremental set and refused for an artifact set. Required, because the snapshot lineage hangs off it and a set's configured identity is source-plus-name, both of which are editable -- if the lineage hung off those, renaming a set would orphan every snapshot it had ever taken and the next run would store a second full copy of the source. Omitted on a create, the service mints one.

repository_domain.description: The repository security boundary this set's snapshots are stored in: one of the repository domains the configuration declares. Required for an incremental set and it has no default, because a default is exactly the decision that must be intentional: a set that silently landed in some "default" repository would be deduplicating against, sharing an encryption key with, sharing a credential with and sharing a corruption fate with whatever else happened to be there.

source_consistency.description: What the operator has arranged around this source while a run reads it. Omitted resolves to live_best_effort, the weakest claim, because inferring quiescence or a frozen image from silence would let a run report a point-in-time snapshot that never existed.

verification_level.description: How far this set's restore points are verified. Omitted resolves to structural, the rung that costs nothing beyond the repository's own metadata; every stronger rung spends a deployment's I/O budget on a cadence, which is not this product's decision to make by default. This is not the artifact validator and the two must not be confused: validator_id checks a durable copy of one file, this is a statement about how hard a snapshot in a repository has been looked at.

verification_sample_percent.description: How much of a snapshot's file content a sampled verification reads, 1 to 100. Omitted takes the engine's own default. A percentage of files rather than of bytes: damage arrives per file, and a byte-proportional sample spends its whole budget inside the largest one.

verification_full_every_seconds.description: How often this set's restore points get a FULL content read regardless of the configured level. A cadence rather than a level, because the deep rungs cost a backup window and the honest shape of "prove it properly sometimes" is a period, not a level somebody sets and turns off again when the nightly window overruns. Omitted means never, which is the only safe default: nobody should acquire a nightly full read by leaving a key out.

verification_restore_drill_every_seconds.description: How often one of this set's restore points gets an actual restore drill. Omitted means never, for verification_full_every_seconds' reason, restated for a cadence that restores the entire source.

source_mount_prefix.description: The leading part of remote_path that is how THIS DEPLOYMENT reaches the source rather than part of the source's own identity: a container bind mount, an install prefix, or the directory an externally-provided snapshot is mounted under for one run. It exists so that moving any of those does not fork the snapshot lineage. Empty is the ordinary case. Declared rather than detected, because nothing on this side can tell which leading segments of a path are the mount, and a heuristic here would be a guess deciding whether a deployment keeps its backup history.

FirstRunStatusResponse.description: GET /system/first-run. The one question a client asks before it decides whether to render the setup flow or the application. Deliberately one field: a client that has just been handed a 503 NOT_CONFIGURED needs to know which screen to show, not why.

configured.description: True once this deployment has a configuration. It never goes back to false for a running process: a live service was opened from a configuration that existed and validated, whatever happens to the file afterwards.

CompleteFirstRunResponse.description: POST /system/first-run. The backup set the first configuration was written around, NESTED rather than flattened, which is the one place this contract deliberately differs from CreateBackupSetResponse beside it. What this operation creates is a whole configuration; the set is its first member, and restart_required is a fact about the instance, not about the set. Keeping backup_set as exactly a BackupSet means a later v1 addition describing the configuration lands beside it instead of becoming indistinguishable from a backup-set field, and can never collide with a field BackupSet itself grows.

restart_required.description: True when the configuration is durably written but this process could not open a service against it in place, so it has to be restarted before it serves the application. Deliberately not an error: setup succeeded, and reporting it as a failure would leave an operator retrying a write that already happened.

Artifact.description: One backup this deployment holds, as the API reports it. Nothing here names an implementation: the fields describe a backup's identity, freshness and trustworthiness, never how it is stored.

backup_set_id.description: The two-part "source/set" identity of the backup set this belongs to.

name.description: The artifact's own filename within its backup set. Always a basename, never a path.

placements.description: Every durable copy this backup currently has, one entry per place. Empty means this backup has no durable copy anywhere yet, which is a real and ordinary answer for one that has only just been discovered or is still transferring; it is never a copy the response failed to describe. local_path above keeps meaning what it always meant, the path ingestion landed on, and is not evidence that a readable file is there: ask the placements.

state.description: The lifecycle state this backup is currently recorded in, e.g. "DISCOVERED", "COMMITTED", "COMPLETE", "QUARANTINED".

size_bytes.description: What the source reported at discovery, or 0 when it reported no size at all.

checksum.description: The hash recorded for the durable local copy at verification. Empty when nothing has been hashed.

validation.description: Whether this backup's content has been validated. Spelled out rather than left as a nullable boolean, so a caller never has to decide what an absent value means.

remote_source_removed_at.description: When the source object was released. Absent while it is still there. Releasing a source is a lifecycle fact, never something a client asks for.

quarantined.description: True when this backup is not trusted and is being held for a human.

quarantine_irrecoverable.description: True when no source remains anywhere to re-ingest from, so retrying cannot help.

quarantine_reason.description: The literal diagnostic sentence recorded at the moment this backup was quarantined (a hash mismatch, a failed content check, or an application validator's rejection). Present for every quarantine cause, not only a validator's. Absent when it is not quarantined, or on the rare row whose quarantining transition carried no detail text.

retention_tier.description: The retention tier that most recently selected this backup to be kept.

retention_policy.description: Which retention policy decides when this backup is deleted. "configured" means its backup set is still configured, so a retention chain selects it and ages it out. "none" means the backup set's configuration was removed while the backup stayed on storage: no chain ever selects it, so nothing here will ever delete it and it holds the space it occupies until somebody removes it by hand. Always sent, and a client must NOT read an absent value as "configured": a response that does not say cannot vouch for either answer, and reading silence as governed is exactly how a backup nothing will ever delete comes to look healthy. A future release may name the policy instead of saying "configured", which is a value change rather than a schema change.

ListArtifactsResponse.description: GET /backups and GET /quarantine. An object with one array field, never a bare top-level array.

ArtifactCheckResponse.description: The verdict of re-checking one quarantined backup. Nothing is written and the backup is not moved: a pass is evidence for an operator deciding whether to retry, not a rehabilitation.

checked.description: False when there was nothing to examine at all, which is still not a pass.

reason.description: What was checked and what it found, already a sentence.

ArtifactReinstateResponse.description: POST /quarantine/{source}/{set}/{name}/reinstate. Re-checks one quarantined backup's durable local copy and, when what it finds is enough, returns it to the state it already held so it counts as a restore point again. `reinstated` and `passed` are separate: `passed` is the verdict of the checks, `reinstated` is whether the backup actually moved. A backup reinstated this way NEVER authorises deleting its remote source again; that forfeiture is permanent and is what makes the action safe to offer.

reinstated.description: Whether the backup was actually returned to a trusted state.

checked.description: Whether there was anything to check at all. False is never a pass.

passed.description: The combined verdict of the checks that ran. A false here is a fact about the backup, not a failed request, and is reported with 200.

state.description: The lifecycle state the backup was returned to, "COMMITTED" or "COMPLETE". Omitted when nothing moved.

reason.description: What was checked and what it found, suitable for showing an operator.

ActivityEvent.description: One recorded lifecycle moment: a backup moved from one state to another. This is a read of the durable, append-only transition record, not a second event stream.

from.description: The state left. Absent for the first transition, since a backup being discovered leaves nothing.

detail.description: What the writer recorded about this move: a quarantine reason, a validator's verdict, an operator's action.

next_cursor.description: The row position this page ended at, to be sent back verbatim as `before` to fetch the events OLDER than the last one above. Present only when this page came back full, so there may be more behind it; absent means the caller has reached the end of the record and asking again would return nothing. It is a decimal token naming a position in the durable lifecycle record, not an opaque blob and not a promise about that record's internal numbering: echo it, do not parse it, and never do arithmetic on it - the only supported use is handing it back unchanged.

ListOperationsResponse.description: GET /operations, newest first. The list counterpart of GET /operations/{id}, for a client that has no operation id to poll with.

BackupSetHealth.description: One backup set's health verdict: whether its backups are fresh and trustworthy, and whether they are on the storage medium its retention policy says they belong on. This is the backup half of health, and it deliberately carries no process or build fact: a running service is not evidence that backups are landing. The placement figures come from durable state rather than from the last pass, so a deployment nobody has run a cycle in front of still reports relocations that have been failing for weeks.

state.description: The verdict. HEALTHY requires positive evidence; silence is never healthy.

reason.description: One operator-facing sentence explaining the state. Never empty: a colour is not an explanation.

halt_reason.description: Why the manager could not connect to this backup set the last time it tried, so no backup ran. HOST_KEY_CHANGED is FR-6's refusal, the host's SSH key no longer matching its known_hosts entry; AUTHENTICATION_FAILED is the host answering and rejecting the login; KEY_PERMISSIONS is a refusal that never reaches the host at all, the configured key's on-disk permissions no longer matching what it was imported with. Absent means no refusal is on record, which is NOT the same claim as the set being reachable: a set that has never been cycled has nothing on record either, and that asymmetry is why this is an optional reason rather than a halted boolean. The refusal is recorded by the cycle that hit it and removed only by a later cycle that ran the set to completion, because re-trusting a changed host key is an explicit administrator action and a cycle that failed for some other reason is not evidence the key verifies again. Reporting it never re-trusts a key, retries a connection, or resumes a set.

newest_good_backup_at.description: The newest trustworthy restore point. Absent when this set has never produced one.

last_completed_backup_at.description: The newest backup that finished, trustworthy or not.

stale_after_seconds.description: The freshness window this set is judged against, in whole seconds, truncated rather than refused. A configuration is only required to make stale_after positive, so a stale_after of 1500ms loads and is reported here as 1, and any window under a second as 0. Zero is therefore a number no configuration could have asked for, and a client that reads one is looking at a window rounded away rather than at a set with no freshness budget. The state and reason beside it were computed from the real duration, not from this number, so the verdict is right even where this field is short.

quarantined_lost_count.description: How many of the quarantined backups have no source left to recover from.

reinstated_remote_retained_count.description: How many backups in this set were re-trusted after quarantine and still hold a remote source this manager has undertaken never to delete. The forfeiture is permanent by design, so this only ever grows, and releasing those remote copies is an operator decision made outside this manager. There is deliberately no companion size: the only measurement this manager ever took of a remote object was at discovery, the producer may since have removed or replaced it, and re-reading every one on every health call would be a network round trip per backup against a source that may be unreachable. The count is known; the bytes are not. Zero here is a real reading, not a missing one, so it is always present.

read_only_retained_count.description: How many backups here currently hold a remote source this manager will never delete because the SET itself is declared read-only (issue #282), not because any one of them was individually reinstated (see reinstated_remote_retained_count, issue #227, for that separate population). Zero is a real reading, not a missing one, so it is always present.

free_bytes.description: Free space at this set's destination. Absent when the reading could not be taken; a zero would otherwise read as "full", which is the one thing it must not be mistaken for.

total_bytes.description: Total capacity at this set's destination, for display beside free_bytes. Absent, like free_bytes, when the reading could not be taken.

storage_level.description: The capacity assessment this destination's free space produced. Absent when no reading could be taken, which is a different thing from OK.

away_from_home.description: How many backups in this set have their durable copy somewhere other than the storage medium this set's retention policy says they belong on. On its own this is not a complaint: a policy pass that has just decided a backup belongs offsite puts it here, and the relocation that carries it there runs in the same pass. Zero is a real reading, not a missing one, so it is always present.

away_from_home_oldest_age_seconds.description: How long the oldest of those copies has existed where it currently sits. Read it for exactly that: it is an upper bound on how long the backup has been in the wrong place, because nothing durable records when a policy last changed where a backup belongs, so a policy edited this morning makes a year-old copy away-from-home this morning and this still reports a year. failed_move_oldest_age_seconds is the figure measured from a moment this manager actually wrote down. Absent when away_from_home is zero: there is nothing for it to be the age of.

unconfirmed_location.description: How many backups in this set could not be placed at all: no durable copy recorded yet, or a relocation in flight leaving two answers to 'where is this'. They are NOT thereby in the right place, and reporting them as if they were is the collapse away_from_home exists to prevent. Zero is a real reading, so it is always present.

open_moves.description: How many relocations this set has that have not finished, in any phase. Zero is a real reading, so it is always present.

open_move_oldest_age_seconds.description: How long the oldest unfinished relocation has been open, whether or not anything has been recorded against it. It is reported separately from failed_move_oldest_age_seconds because not every way a relocation gets stuck leaves a reason behind: the refusal that fires immediately before the original copy is deleted deliberately changes nothing at all, so such a relocation is open and not failed, and this is the figure that still grows. It changes no state, because 'open for a while' has no honest threshold: a single large copy can legitimately outlast one cycle. Absent when open_moves is zero.

failed_moves.description: How many unfinished relocations had their last attempt fail. This is the one figure here that turns an otherwise-healthy backup set DEGRADED, and it is what makes a week of failing relocations reach this endpoint at all: everything else about a relocation's outcome describes a single pass and is gone by the time anybody reads a status page. Zero is a real reading, so it is always present.

failed_move_oldest_age_seconds.description: How long the oldest failing relocation has been open, measured from when this manager wrote it down. It is the difference between a blip and a wedge: a transient failure clears on the next cycle, and one that does not turns this into days and then weeks. Absent when failed_moves is zero.

failed_move_reason.description: What was recorded against that oldest failing relocation. Served beside the count rather than instead of it, because a count alone cannot tell an operator whether to look at a storage policy, a credential or a network, and this sentence is the only account of the failure that outlives the pass that hit it. Absent when failed_moves is zero.

HealthResponse.description: GET /system/health. Every configured backup set's freshness verdict, computed fresh on every call. Build and process facts are GET /system/version's, deliberately not restated here.

CatalogFailure.description: One recovery manifest a catalog pass could not use.

path.description: The manifest that failed. Reported because it is the only thing that identifies which one needs attention, and an operator with server access is this failure's only audience.

CatalogReportResponse.description: POST /catalog/scan and POST /catalog/rebuild. Both return this shape, because a scan is the rebuild with nothing written: a preview computed by a second implementation would be a preview of something else.

dry_run.description: True for a scan. Nothing was written.

scanned.description: Every recovery manifest examined, whatever the verdict.

reconstructed.description: How many records were, or for a scan would be, rebuilt.

already_present.description: How many were already known and left untouched.

SetEnabledRequest.description: POST /backup-sets/{source}/{set}/enabled. A disabled backup set is excluded from every run cycle and nothing already backed up is touched, which is why this is state-changing but not destructive.

SetReadOnlyRequest.description: POST /backup-sets/{source}/{set}/read-only. Declares, or withdraws, a backup set's read-only status (issue #282). Turning it on only prevents a future deletion; turning it back off does not retroactively authorise deleting anything already retained under it, so this is state-changing but not destructive.

UpdateBackupSetRequest.description: PATCH /backup-sets/{source}/{set}. A SPARSE edit of one already-persisted backup set (issue #350): every property is optional, and a property this body omits is left exactly as it is rather than cleared. That is what lets the Web UI's per-box Save persist only the box it belongs to. It deliberately carries no name/source_name: a backup set's identity keys every journal row, artifact id and recovery manifest it has ever produced, so a rename is a migration rather than an edit. It does carry ssh_key_id and known_hosts_line (issue #572), because a key replaced on the source host and a host key that changes when a server is rebuilt are both ordinary events a set has to be able to be told about, and until they were here the only route was to remove the set and create it again. Both are still references produced by the import and probe steps rather than material typed here, and re-trusting a host is still a trust decision, which is what acknowledge_host_key_change is for.

port.description: 0 selects the default port, so this is a meaningful value rather than an absent one; omit the property entirely to leave the port alone.
