completion_strategy.description: This and stable_for_seconds are one setting spelled as two properties, and a body moving to "stable" has to carry both: a backup set whose strategy is "stable" and whose window is zero is refused here exactly as it is at creation, and there is no default for the server to supply, because too short a window copies a half-written file.

stable_for_seconds.description: Required, and only stored, when the completion strategy in effect after this edit is "stable"; an edit that leaves the strategy as anything else clears it, so that an operator's file never holds a number nothing reads. A body naming a window the resulting configuration would therefore NOT hold is refused with INVALID_REQUEST rather than accepted and cleared (issue #572): a 200 for a write that was discarded is an answer other things get built on. Sending 0 alongside a move off "stable" is not refused, because that asks for exactly what happens.

ssh_key_id.description: The id of a key POST /ssh-keys has already imported, replacing whichever key this backup set authenticates with now (issue #572). A reference, never key material, exactly as on the create path. An id no import produced is refused with SSH_KEY_NOT_FOUND and nothing is written.

known_hosts_line.description: The exact known_hosts line this backup set should trust from now on, as POST /backup-sets/probe-host-key returns it (issue #572). Replacing it is how a set is told that its source host was legitimately rebuilt. It pins ONE plain host key: a line carrying a marker such as @cert-authority is refused as an invalid request, because trusting whatever a key vouches for is a different decision from trusting a server and the fingerprint comparison this edit shows cannot describe it. The line must also name this backup set's own host, at the port this edit leaves it on, or it is refused: one naming a different host parses and fingerprints exactly like one naming this one, and pinning it would leave the set unable to verify its host at all. A line that changes what the set trusts for its own address is refused with BACKUP_SET_HOST_KEY_CHANGE_NOT_ACKNOWLEDGED unless acknowledge_host_key_change is set, in both directions: a different key being pinned, and a key on record that this one line would stop pinning (a host answering with more than one key algorithm has a known_hosts line each). Re-sending the line already trusted, when it is the only one on record, changes no trust and is never refused.

validator_id.description: An id from the registered validator catalog GET /validators serves, or "" for none. Never a path.

acknowledge_repoint.description: Confirms that this edit is meant to point the backup set at different data. Required only when the body actually changes host, remote_path or local_path on a set that already has artifacts on record; without it such an edit is refused with BACKUP_SET_REPOINT_NOT_ACKNOWLEDGED and nothing is written. It is not a property of the backup set and nothing persists it: it answers one refusal, for one request.

acknowledge_host_key_change.description: Confirms that this edit is meant to change what host keys this backup set trusts for its own address (issue #572). Required when known_hosts_line pins a different key from the one on record, and equally when it would stop pinning one that IS on record; without it the edit is refused with BACKUP_SET_HOST_KEY_CHANGE_NOT_ACKNOWLEDGED, naming the fingerprint on record and the one being offered, and nothing is written. Changing remote.port does not exempt an edit from this: a port is how you reach the same machine, so a set that pins a key for host:22 is still having its trust changed by a line that pins something else for host:2222. Separate from acknowledge_repoint on purpose: that one answers "this is the same data at a new address" and this one answers "this is the same host with a new key", and one flag for both would let an operator who meant one of them quietly grant the other.

skip_connection_check.description: Writes this edit without proving the connection first (issue #624). An edit that changes host, port, user, ssh_key_id, known_hosts_line or remote_path is checked against the source before it is written, and refused with BACKUP_SET_CONNECTION_NOT_PROVEN when the check fails; this is the deliberate opt-out, and a set written under it is marked connection_unverified until a test passes. The check is made here rather than by the caller because a sparse edit plus a set whose trust anchor this API never publishes is not something a caller can assemble a candidate out of. Omitted or false checks, which is what every edit that changes a connection field should do.

poll_interval_seconds.description: Change how often this set's source is checked. Absent leaves it alone; an explicit 0 means "inherit the deployment default again", which is unambiguous because SettingsSchema.service.min_poll_interval_seconds makes zero a value no caller could be asking for.

source_consistency.description: Change what the operator has arranged around this source. Editable after creation because the arrangement genuinely changes -- a database gets a pre-backup quiesce hook, a filesystem gets LVM snapshots -- and the set should be able to say so without being recreated.

verification_level.description: Change how far this set's restore points are verified.

verification_sample_percent.description: Change the sampled verification's size, 1 to 100.

verification_full_every_seconds.description: Change the full-content-read cadence; 0 means never.

verification_restore_drill_every_seconds.description: Change the restore-drill cadence; 0 means never.

RunningWork.description: What a run cycle is doing for one backup set right now (issue #350). It is the content of the warning shown before edit mode opens: discarding a partial transfer of a named artifact is a materially different cost from cancelling a scheduler tick that has not started work, and only a message saying which one it is lets an operator decide.

artifact.description: The artifact being worked on, or "" during discovery, when the cycle has reached this set but not yet picked one.

BackupSetEditHoldState.description: GET /backup-sets/{source}/{set}/edit-hold. What entering edit mode for this backup set would interrupt, and whether a hold is already in force. `running` is null when no cycle is currently inside this set, which is what lets a client open edit mode with no prompt for a risk that does not exist.

expires_at.description: When the hold lapses if nothing renews it. Present only when held.

BackupSetEditHold.description: POST /backup-sets/{source}/{set}/edit-hold. The lease just taken or renewed, plus what taking it interrupted. `stopped` is null when nothing was running, so a client never claims to have stopped something it did not.

expires_at.description: When this hold lapses if nothing renews it. A client that means to keep editing renews well before it.

RetentionOverride.description: One backup set's OWN retention policy, exactly as its configuration file carries it: unresolved, with every omitted field still omitted. An override names the WHOLE chain (a tiers list, or all three of daily_days, weekly_months and monthly_months) and half a chain is refused, because completing the missing half from the product defaults is how a set silently ends up retaining less than the operator who wrote the deployment's policy believes. Everything that is not the chain inherits from the deployment's resolved policy when omitted, so an override that names no timezone is reckoned in the deployment's, not in UTC.

week_starts_on.description: Absent inherits the deployment's week start.

daily_days.description: FR-18's original three-scalar chain. All three or none.

tiers.description: FR-18's general chain, mutually exclusive with the three scalars above. An explicitly empty list is refused rather than applied: emptying a chain reinstates the default daily/weekly/monthly policy rather than keeping nothing.

protect_last_known_good.description: Absent inherits the deployment's FR-19 posture.

acknowledge_medium_disclosure.description: The operator's acknowledgment of the storage-medium disclosure (SettingsSchema.storage.medium_disclosure), on this write for the reason UpdateSettingsRequest carries it: an override is a whole chain and can send a tier's artifacts to a non-local medium exactly as the deployment's policy can. Required on, and only on, a write that maps a tier to a medium the chain currently deciding for this set does not already map it to; without it that write is refused with MEDIUM_DISCLOSURE_REQUIRED. It is a consent and not part of the policy: never written to the file, and never present on the override half of a response.

BackupSetRetention.description: Which retention policy one backup set is retained under, and where that policy came from. All of it is served together because 'what is deciding' and 'is that this set's own or the deployment's' are one question for an operator reading a preview that is about to delete something, and answering it in two calls is how a surface shows a chain beside the wrong attribution.

is_override.description: True when this set declares its own policy. It is reported rather than derived by comparing the two chains: a set that deliberately pinned a chain identical to the deployment's is NOT inheriting, and the whole point of pinning it is that a later edit to the deployment's policy will not move it.

Placement.description: One DURABLE copy of one backup, and where it actually is (EPIC E, FR-29). A placement exists because the journal recorded a finished copy, so the ABSENCE of a placement is the absence of a copy: a transfer still in flight has no placement at all, and neither does a copy this deployment has released. That is deliberate, and it is what lets a surface tell "there is no copy here" apart from "there is a copy here nobody can confirm", which is what the access and verification_class fields are for. Nothing here is a price, a bill or an estimate of how long a restore will take; see access.

medium.description: "local" for the backup set's own directory on this machine, or the id of a configured storage medium. "local" is reserved: a configured medium can never claim it.

medium_type.description: What kind of place holds this copy. Served rather than left to a client comparing the medium id against the literal "local", so one product decides what local means.

location.description: Where the copy is, in the terms of the place that holds it: an absolute path for a local copy, an object key for a medium copy. Never a credential, never a signed URL.

size_bytes.description: What this copy measures. ABSENT when nobody recorded it, which is not zero: a backup can genuinely be empty, and a client must not render the two the same way.

storage_class.description: The storage class this copy is written with, already resolved. Absent for a local copy, which has no such thing.

verification_class.description: The strongest verification this copy has ACHIEVED, never the strongest one configured (FR-31). ABSENT means nothing has verified this copy at all, which is a different fact from a weak pass and must never be rendered as one.

verified_at.description: When verification_class was last achieved. Absent exactly when verification_class is.

access.description: Whether this copy can be read right now, from the closed vocabulary FR-34 defines, derived only from facts this product holds. "immediate": readable on demand. "requires_restore": the storage class has to be restored first, which takes hours the provider does not predict. "restoring": a restore has been asked for; the provider reports no percentage, so none is shown. "unreachable": this deployment cannot currently reach the place holding the copy, which is emphatically not the same statement as the copy being gone.

status.description: ACTIVE means the copy is meant to be there. DELETE_PENDING means a delete has been decided and durably recorded and may not have happened yet, so the bytes are probably still there and are on their way out. There is no third value here: a copy the journal knows is gone is not served at all, because a row for it would read as a copy.

StorageMediumSummary.description: One configured storage medium, as the settings surface reports it: what it is called, what kind of place it is, which bucket and region, and which storage class artifacts are written with. There is deliberately no field here for key material of any kind, and there never will be (FR-33). A credential reaches this product only as a reference to a file, an environment variable or a command, and none of those three has a spelling on this boundary at all. That absence now covers the WRITE direction too (POST/PUT below), and it extends to the credential's KIND: there is no field saying whether a medium reads a file, a variable or a command, because where a credential comes from is a fact about the manager's host that an API caller has no use for. An edit therefore does not have to resupply the credential; omitting it keeps the one already configured.

id.description: How a retention tier names this medium.

type.description: What kind of place this is. `s3` is a bucket an operator declared in storage_mediums. `local` is the drive this deployment's backups land on, which is not declared anywhere: it is synthesised from the configuration, it is what every retention tier that names no destination means, and it is always in this list (#622). Branch on is_local rather than on this word: the set grows by architecture decision, and a second local-ish backend added here one day must not silently make an entry undeletable.

storage_class.description: The class objects are written with, already resolved, so a client never has to know what an unset value defaults to.

reads_require_restore.description: True when this medium's storage class cannot be read on demand: anything already here, and anything a tier sends here, needs an explicit restore taking hours before it can be read at all. Computed from the storage class by the engine rather than restated by a client, so one product decides what archive means.

endpoint.description: The endpoint override, for an S3-compatible service. Empty means the provider's own endpoint for the region.

prefix.description: The key namespace inside the bucket. Empty puts the key layout at the root.

upload_verification.description: How an upload is proven before the local copy is deleted, already resolved, so a client never has to know what an unset value defaults to. readback re-downloads and re-hashes; attested asks the endpoint for its own whole-object digest, which no s3 backend can currently serve.

path.description: The drive the LOCAL destination writes to, resolved exactly as the capacity section resolves its backup root so one deployment cannot report two mounts. Empty for a declared medium, because a bucket has no path on the manager's host, and empty for a local entry this configuration cannot place yet (no backup set configured, or sets on genuinely different volumes), which a surface renders as "not known yet" rather than as a blank path.

is_local.description: True for the one entry that is the drive this deployment's backups land on (#622). It is not declared in the configuration and cannot be edited or removed, so a surface reads this rather than comparing an id against a reserved string it would have to hold its own copy of.

is_default.description: True for the destination a NEWLY CREATED retention tier starts on. Exactly one entry in a list carries it. It says nothing about where anything currently is: moving it moves no backup and rewrites no tier, which is why it is one click and carries no disclosure (#622).

connection_unverified.description: Whether this storage destination was declared without ever having been proven (issue #636). True means a caller deliberately skipped a check it could have run, which is `medium add --no-verify` and `skip_connection_check` and nothing else; a test connection that PASSES against it clears the mark, and one that fails leaves it alone. ABSENT is not "unverified": every configuration written before this field existed says nothing, an engine built before it answers nothing, and a client that read silence as a mark would declare every destination on every deployment unproven on the first upgrade. Read absence as "nothing here says this was skipped". Always absent for the local hard drive, which is not declared and has no bucket to prove.

VerificationClassInfo.description: One rung of the verification ladder (FR-31), with what it proves and what achieving it takes, in the engine's own words. Served rather than transcribed into a frontend, for the reason the retention schema is served: a surface holding its own copy of what "existence" proves eventually says something the engine does not.

proves.description: What achieving this class actually establishes.

requires.description: What achieving this class requires, in words. Deliberately words and not a number, and deliberately not a field called cost: this product has no price list and no negotiated rates, so a figure here would be invented, and a field named for one is one release away from holding one. The contract's no-cost gate refuses that name, and this field is not an exception to it.

downloads_object.description: True when achieving this class downloads the object's bytes, which the provider bills as egress. It is the same predicate the engine refuses automatic revalidation on, not a second note kept in step by hand.

StorageSchema.description: The closed value sets and the consent text a storage-medium mapping is written against, served rather than transcribed into a frontend.

medium_disclosure.description: The consent text an operator has to be shown before the first save that sends a retention tier's artifacts to a non-local medium (FR-27). It names the deletion consequence, and the write is refused without an acknowledgment, so this is the words behind a refusal rather than a label a client could reword.

retrieval_disclosure.description: The plain statement about reading a copy back off a storage medium. It carries no figure, because this product cannot compute one honestly.

CycleMoveOutcome.description: What a finished cycle's move pass got done: how many artifacts were due to move to the medium their retention tier names, and how many arrived. Without these, a cycle in which every move was refused is indistinguishable from one in which every move landed, which is the same defect artifacts_walked and artifacts_through exist to remove one layer down. There is no reason string here, deliberately: the engine's own refusal sentence is built from whatever the transport handed back, about an endpoint, a bucket and a credential reference, so it stays on the terminal and in the event stream and never on this boundary.

attempted.description: How many artifacts the move pass took up: a move it resumed, a move it planned, or a plan it refused outright.

landed.description: How many of those reached their home medium with the source gone, which is the only outcome that is a move.

CycleOutcome.description: What a finished run cycle actually got done, read off the operation's own recorded summary. A cycle "completed" when it ran to the end, which is a narrower statement than anyone reading it assumes: an artifact's own quarantine is a business outcome and not an operation failure, so a cycle that backed nothing up finishes looking exactly like one that backed everything up. These counts are what tell the two apart.

artifacts_walked.description: How many backups the cycle had a reason to touch.

artifacts_through.description: How many of those ended the cycle with their bytes on durable storage.

moves.description: What this cycle's move pass got done, absent when the recorded summary does not carry it. Absent is not a pair of zeroes: a cycle recorded by a build that did not write these has not moved nothing, it has not said. A deployment that declares no storage medium records a real pair of zeroes, which reads as nothing to do.

RestoreOperationRequest.description: The restore_placement action's own parameters. Present only when action is restore_placement, and refused when it is not: a body carrying restore parameters for a run_cycle is a request that has confused two operations, and answering it cheerfully is how the expensive version of the same mistake gets made later.

artifact_id.description: The backup whose copy is to be restored, as source/set/name.

medium.description: The id of the storage medium holding the copy to restore.

window_days.description: How many days the restored copy should stay readable. Bounded to 1 to 30: zero is not a shorter restore, it is one that is billed and then immediately unavailable, and a fat-fingered large number is a month of double billing.

acknowledged.description: The operator saying, in one field, that they know a restore costs money and takes hours. Required true. It is the opposite of a force flag: the value that costs nothing is the default, so a caller that forgot to ask a human gets a refusal rather than a bill.

OperationRestore.description: A restore operation's own facts: what was asked for, which never changes, and where it has actually got to, which is re-derived from the storage provider on every read rather than remembered. Absent on every other action. There is no percentage field, no completion-time field and no cost field: S3 reports a restore as running or finished and nothing else, and this product holds no price list, so any of the three would be invented.

access.description: What can be done with the copy right now: immediate, requires_restore, restoring, or unreachable. Empty when the medium could not be asked at all.

detail.description: The plain-words sentence a surface prints beside access. Never a percentage, a finishing time or a price.

restored_until.description: When the provider says the restored copy stops being readable. Omitted, never zero-valued, while the provider reports none: it is shown when S3 reports it and nothing is invented in its place until then.

wait.description: The storage class's OWN published restore time, in plain words. A documented property of the class, and never an estimate for this particular restore.

billing.description: The statement that a bill exists, with no amount, because this deployment holds no price list and an invented number is worse than none.

MediumPreflightCheck.description: One step of a storage-medium preflight. There is deliberately no field here for key material of any kind, and there never will be (FR-33): `detail` is one of the engine's own sentences, never the text of what actually came back, because that names a path on the host or the name of an environment variable. The classified cause goes to this manager's log instead.

step.description: What this step proves. `credentials` is whether the credential the medium declares can be obtained at all, which is a question for the host; `reach` is whether the endpoint answers and holds the bucket with that credential, which is a question for the provider. `deliverable` is whether an artifact can be delivered to this medium's storage class at all: an archive class cannot take delivery, and is refused without writing anything, because a probe object there is billed for a minimum duration measured in months. `write`, `read_back` and `delete` are a real object written, read back byte for byte and removed again, because read access is not what a move needs and a write nobody can read is not a backup. `storage_class` is whether the object came back in the class the configuration asked for. `verification` is whether the class this medium's upload_verification declares can actually be achieved here, asked of the endpoint rather than looked up.

outcome.description: `skipped` is a real answer and not a quiet pass: it means an earlier step failed in a way that makes this one meaningless. A surface that renders a skipped write as anything but "this was never tried" has told an operator their bucket is writable on the strength of a credential that was never obtained.

category.description: The transport category a failure classified as, absent when the step did not fail. It is the machine-readable half: a client branches on this and never on `detail`.

detail.description: What this step found, in words, for a person to act on.

MediumPreflightResponse.description: The result of proving one storage medium works. The preflight writes a small probe object to the medium, reads it back byte for byte, checks the storage class it landed in against the one the configuration claims, asks whether the verification class the medium declares can actually be achieved there, and deletes the probe. That is deliberately more than a reachability ping: a wrong region, a policy that denies PutObject and an endpoint that silently ignores storage_class all answer a ping perfectly well and then fail a move, in the middle of a cycle, after an artifact has already been chosen to leave local disk. A medium that does not work is a 200 with `ok` false, not an error: a bucket that is not there is what an operator did, not what broke, exactly as a failed backup-set connection test reports itself. The operation takes an id and never a candidate medium, unlike that connection test: a medium is declared in the configuration file and nowhere else, and the only fields that would make a candidate one meaningful are the three credential references, so a request body for one would make a path on this host into something an API caller sends (FR-33). Nothing schedules this; it is a real side effect on somebody's bucket and it runs only because a person asked.

medium.description: The medium id this ran against.

checks.description: One entry per step, in the order the engine performs them. Always the full list, so a surface renders a fixed set of rows rather than discovering which steps happened to run.

RetryFailedRequest.description: POST /backups/{source}/{set}/{name}/retry's optional body. Everything about the retry is decided by the backup's own recorded state, so there is nothing here that changes what happens: the note is recorded alongside the transition so a later failure of the same backup carries the context of what was tried last time, rather than only that something was.

note.description: An operator's own explanation for why this retry is worth making ("replaced the failing credential", "the NAS came back").

LiveActivityField.description: One field of an event, rendered as a string and already redacted. A pair rather than a map because the order the event logged its fields in is the order that reads best, and because a client rendering a line wants them in that order without sorting.

LiveActivityAction.description: One action that started and has not reported an outcome. It is what makes "this announced itself and went quiet" something a surface can say, rather than something an operator would have to notice by reading every line and remembering which starts they had seen. An action still legitimately running appears here too, and that is correct rather than a false alarm: the honest sentence is "started four minutes ago and has not reported an outcome", and whether four minutes is long is a judgement the person reading it is far better placed to make than this service is.

action.description: The action's stable name, as its two lines carry it.

action_id.description: What the start and its missing completion would be paired by.

started_at.description: When the start line was emitted, which is the only thing anything can work out how long it has been quiet from.

sequence.description: The start line's own sequence, so a client can find the line this is about in the tail it already holds.

LiveActivityDeployment.description: The log that belongs to no single backup set, served in its own right rather than copied onto every set's feed. A cycle starting covers every set and a capacity check is about a filesystem, so neither belongs on one set's strip; until this bucket existed the only alternatives were dropping those lines (which hides them) or reporting them on every strip, and the second is what shipped, so on a real deployment every set's strip showed the same log and the shared lines crowded out each set's own. It is absent when the caller narrowed the reading to one backup set, because a caller that named a set asked about that set. It is present, and is the whole answer, for a deployment with no configured backup sets at all, which is exactly when a new operator is pressing buttons in a wizard and has nothing else to read.

unfinished_actions.description: Every action belonging to no single backup set whose start is still held with no completion behind it, oldest first. It is deliberately NOT filtered by the cursor: a cursor asks what is new, and an action that has been quiet for ten minutes is not new, so a client polling all along would otherwise be told about it once and never again. It is derived from the tail this process is still holding rather than tracked in a structure of its own, so an action whose start has scrolled out of the bounded buffer is forgotten along with every other line from that far back.

truncated.description: Whether the limit cut this reading short and the rest is still held. Always present rather than omitted when false: a client reading an absent key as "nothing is missing" reads a server that stopped sending it the same way, and silence about a gap is what this feed must never do.

dropped.description: Whether lines this caller's cursor had not reached yet fell out of the bounded buffer before this read did. They are gone, and the tail above is not continuous with whatever the caller already holds.

oldest_sequence.description: The oldest sequence still held in this bucket, which is a bound on the buffer and not on the slice above.

latest_sequence.description: The newest sequence still held in this bucket.

LiveActivityEvent.description: One line of the live feed. It carries the engine's own event name, the engine's own severity and the event's own fields, because what a moment is worth calling is presentation and belongs to whichever client is presenting: a severity invented on the way to the wire would freeze one screen's display decision for every other client. The level is not such a decision, it is what the emitter chose when it decided a line was a warning rather than a note, so it is carried through rather than re-derived.

sequence.description: Strictly increasing across every event this process has emitted, so a client can order a set's own lines against the deployment-wide ones and resume from the last one it saw.

level.description: The severity the engine emitted this event at, carried through unchanged.

result.description: How the operation this line reports WENT, stated by the engine rather than re-derived by whoever draws the line. It is not a second spelling of level and it is carried for the same reason level is: the emitter said it. There is no success severity and there cannot be one, because a level is an ordering every reader treats as a threshold, so before this field existed a completion that went well arrived at info and was indistinguishable from a note, and every client wanting to draw one as good news re-derived it from event names and lifecycle state values with anything it did not recognise silently staying neutral. It is called result and not outcome on purpose: connection_test carries a field of its own called outcome, and LiveActivitySet.outcome in this same response is a different vocabulary again, so a client reading set.outcome beside set.events[i].result is told those are different questions. Absent is a real answer rather than a default: a start has not gone any way yet, and an ordinary progress note reports no operation at all.

action.description: The stable name of the operator-visible action this line opens or closes (cycle, connection_test). Absent on every line that is neither half of a pair.

action_id.description: What an action's start and its completion are paired by, structurally rather than by the habit of spelling one event cycle_start and the other cycle_end. A line carrying this and no outcome is a start; one carrying both is that start's completion. It is what lets a reader notice an action that announced itself and then went quiet, which is the state an operator most needs named and the one nothing could see.

event.description: The engine's own event name (discovery, lifecycle_transition, transfer_stats, retention, cycle_end and the rest). It is deliberately not an enum: the catalog grows, and a client that meets a name it has no special rendering for prints the message and the fields, which is a worse line rather than a broken one.

scope.description: Whether this event belongs to the backup set carrying it or to the deployment. Most events name their own set, or an artifact that names one. A few genuinely do not: a cycle starting covers every set. Those are carried in the response's deployment bucket rather than on any set's feed, so a set's feed answers what that set is doing and the deployment's answers what the whole system is doing. The sequence numbers are one counter across both, so a client holding both can interleave them exactly where they happened.

LiveActivitySet.description: What one backup set is doing right now, and the tail of events behind it. Every configured set appears whether or not anything has happened to it: a panel that shows up only during activity teaches an operator to hunt for it, and its absence then means either nothing is running or nothing is reporting, with no way to tell which.

active.description: Whether a cycle is inside this set in the serving process right now. It is a separate fact from the fraction below and both are needed: a large artifact holds the numbers still for a long time while everything is fine, so a fraction alone cannot tell slow from stuck. This is what a moving indicator is driven by.

stage.description: The step the artifact below is at. Absent when nothing is in flight.

artifact.description: The artifact the stage is about. Absent when nothing is in flight.

artifacts_completed.description: How many artifacts this set's current or most recent pass has finished driving forward.

artifacts_total.description: How many artifacts that pass set out to drive forward. Absent until the pass has counted them, which is a different answer from zero: zero of zero draws as a finished cycle, and that is the reading an operator would act on wrongly.

progress_basis.description: What the fraction counts, said rather than left to be inferred. It counts artifacts: artifacts done over artifacts this pass will walk, which is a fraction of two numbers the engine actually holds. It jumps unevenly on a set mixing a 2GB dump with a 4KB text file, and that is honest; the smoother alternative is a byte total that does not exist until discovery has finished and that no remote reports reliably even then. unknown is the window before the pass has counted, and it is why artifacts_total is absent rather than zero.

bytes_per_second.description: The three byte counters describe the ONE artifact named above, never the set, and are absent whenever no copy is in flight and reporting, which is a different fact from a measured zero. There is deliberately no time-remaining figure beside them: everything needed to work one out for the artifact in flight is here, and a figure the engine cannot check does not belong on a wire other clients then have to serve.

failures.description: How many of this set's artifacts ended this pass in a terminal failure state. It describes the pass, not the set's history, so it resets when a new pass begins: last night's two failures are not tonight's, and a strip carrying them forward would keep an operator looking at a problem already dealt with.

outcome.description: How this set's last finished pass ENDED, which is a different fact from how many of its artifacts failed. A pass whose reconcile or discovery failed never reaches an artifact at all, so it leaves failures at zero and artifacts_total absent, and a strip reading only those two would draw it as a set that has nothing to do. stopped is a pass an operator stopped (an edit hold, a cancellation) and is deliberately not failed: in a product whose job is to be believed about backups, spelling an ordinary edit the same way as a source that has gone unreachable is a false alarm. Absent until a pass has ended here.

finished_at.description: When the pass this strip describes started and ended. Both absent until a pass has actually run here; finished_at is absent while one is running.

events.description: The tail, oldest first, filtered by whatever cursor the caller sent. Empty is an empty array, never an absent key.

unfinished_actions.description: Every action inside this backup set whose start is still held with no completion behind it, oldest first. It is deliberately NOT filtered by the cursor: a cursor asks what is new, and an action that has been quiet for ten minutes is not new, so a client polling all along would otherwise be told about it once and never again. It is derived from the tail this process is still holding rather than tracked in a structure of its own, so an action whose start has scrolled out of the bounded buffer is forgotten along with every other line from that far back.

truncated.description: Whether limit cut this reading short. The events above are the OLDEST held that are newer than the cursor, never the newest, because a cursor a client advances past a gap is a client that never sees the middle of a burst again. True means the rest is still held: ask again with the sequence this reading ends at.

dropped.description: Whether lines this cursor had not reached yet fell out of the bounded buffer before this read did. True means the tail above is not continuous with what the caller already holds, and a client should say so rather than presenting a gap as continuity. The full record is the durable feed at GET /activity.

latest_sequence.description: The bounds of what the server still holds for this set, NOT of the events array above. The buffer is bounded on purpose, so a client whose cursor has fallen below oldest_sequence knows it missed lines and can say so instead of presenting a gap as continuity. The full history is the durable record at GET /activity.

LiveActivityResponse.description: One reading of the live feed. It is a snapshot a client polls, not a stream: this product runs on a NAS behind whatever reverse proxy the operator already had, and behind the UI container's own proxy in the two-container topology, so a held-open response is at the mercy of every buffering and idle-timeout default in that path. A plain GET works through all of them, needs no reconnection logic, and is exactly as readable from a terminal as from a browser. The cursor on the request is what keeps polling cheap.

epoch.description: An opaque name for the process this reading came from. It changes on every start, and the sequence counter the cursor is built from starts again at zero with it, so a client that kept polling across a restart would otherwise ask for everything after a sequence the new process has not reached yet and be told, correctly and uselessly, that there is nothing new. Compare it with the one the last reading carried: a different value means drop the cursor and everything held behind it, because the cycle those lines described no longer exists.

poll_after_ms.description: How long the server suggests waiting before asking again. The server decides because the server is the one that knows whether anything is moving: a client picking its own interval would either hammer a NAS holding a dozen idle sets or watch a transfer at a cadence that makes the bar jump.

deployment.description: The deployment-wide log: the events that name no single backup set. Absent when the reading was narrowed to one backup set.

SSHKey.description: One key in this deployment's own key store. It carries no server-side path: SSHKeyRef.KeyFile is kept off the wire so a caller never learns this process's filesystem layout, and an inventory is not an exception to that. What travels instead is the id, the public half's algorithm and SHA256 fingerprint, the authorized_keys line, and which backup sets point at it.

id.description: The store id. This is the value POST /ssh-keys returned when the key was imported, the value BackupSetSpec.ssh_key_id takes, and the value `retnd backup-set patch --ssh-key-id` takes.

algorithm.description: The public half's algorithm, or empty when the key could not be described (see problem).

fingerprint.description: The SHA256 fingerprint, in the form `ssh-keygen -lf` prints, or empty when the key could not be described.

public_key.description: The authorized_keys line for this key. Public material by definition, and the one string here an operator has to be able to copy: a verification that reaches the host, matches its key and then fails to authenticate is fixed by pasting exactly this into the remote account's authorized_keys.

imported_at.description: RFC 3339, or empty when this deployment cannot report it. Never omitted, so a caller can tell an unknown time from a build that does not report one.

passphrase_protected.description: This key needs a passphrase to be usable, so it is listed and cannot be verified until that passphrase resolves.

problem.description: Why this row could not be described. Never names a path.

used_by.description: Every backup set id pointing at this key, sorted. Never omitted: "used by nothing" is a real answer, and it is the column that turns a wall of ids into a decision.

ListSSHKeysResponse.description: GET /ssh-keys. The read this API never had: an imported key's id used to cross the wire exactly once, in the response to the POST that created it, so ssh_key_id took a value nothing in the product would tell anybody.

SSHKeyCandidate.description: One private key file this engine can actually see. Unlike SSHKey, this DOES carry a path, because a candidate's path is its identity to an operator and there is no other way to say which of several files is meant. What makes that safe is that the locations searched are a closed, constant set decided server-side, never caller-supplied and never walked recursively. The handle travelling back is the opaque id, never the path.

id.description: The opaque handle ImportSSHKeyFromCandidateRequest.candidate_id takes. Derived from the path, so it needs no server-side state, and not a path, so no request can name a file for this process to read.

algorithm.description: Read from the .pub beside the private key, and empty when there is none. Never derived by reading the private key.

fingerprint.description: Read from the .pub beside the private key, and empty when there is none. A candidate with no fingerprint is listed and is not selectable, because deriving one would mean reading a private key in order to describe it in a list.

public_key.description: The .pub's own line, or empty when there is none.

mode.description: The private file's permission bits as an operator would write them, for example "0600".

in_store.description: A key with this fingerprint is already in the key store, so selecting it here would make a second copy of something already on the other list.

in_store_id.description: That key's store id when in_store is true, so a client can offer the existing key instead of a duplicate import.

selectable.description: Whether this candidate can be chosen. See reason when it cannot.

reason.description: Why this candidate is not selectable. A row an operator cannot pick and cannot explain is worse than no row.

SSHKeyDiscoveryLocation.description: One place the scan looked, reported whether or not anything was found there. Every location is always reported, including the absent ones: an empty candidate list has two readings, "you have no keys" and "I could not look where your keys are", and on a packaged install the engine is a distroless container with five mounts and no home directory, so the second is the true one.

kind.description: Why this location is in the set at all, so a client can render "the key file your configuration names" differently from "a directory that is not mounted in this container". One of configured-key-file, mount, home, discovery-dir.

found.description: How many candidates came from here.

problem.description: Why nothing could be read from here. Empty when the location was read.

ListSSHKeyCandidatesResponse.description: GET /ssh/key-candidates. The locations travel beside the candidates, in one response, so a client cannot render one without the other.

StorageMediumCredentialsReference.description: Where one storage medium's credentials come from. Exactly one of the four must be set, and none of them is credential MATERIAL: this is a reference in all four spellings. credentials_id is the one a browser uses, because it is the only one that names nothing about the manager's host.

credentials_id.description: An id an earlier POST /storage-credentials returned. It resolves, server-side, to the 0600 file that import wrote beside the configuration, and that file's path is what the configuration ends up naming. This is the spelling to use from a browser: it is opaque, it names no path and no variable on the manager's host, and it is therefore safe on a request body, in an echoed command line and in an exported terminal transcript.

file.description: A path to an AWS shared-credentials file on the manager's host. The preferred source when an operator already has one, because rclone opens the file itself and the secret never enters the manager's process at all.

env.description: The NAME of an environment variable the credentials are read from at connection time. Never a value.

command.description: An argv array whose stdout is the credentials, run directly and never through a shell. This is how a secrets manager is adopted without this product depending on one.

StorageMediumRequest.description: One storage destination as a caller describes it: for POST /storage-mediums (declare it), PUT /storage-mediums/{id} (replace its description) and POST /storage-mediums/preflight (prove it before either). The same shape for all three deliberately, so what is proven and what is saved cannot be different destinations. There is no field here for credential material, and there never will be (FR-33): the credentials block names a reference.

id.description: lower_snake_case, unique, and not `local`, which is reserved. This is the name a retention tier will use.

region.description: The provider region, passed to the backend unexamined. This product deliberately holds no list of legal regions: it would be a second, staler copy that refuses a region that works.

endpoint.description: An endpoint override for an S3-compatible service. Empty means the provider's own endpoint for the region. A wizard's provider preset only fills this field in.

bucket.description: The bucket artifacts are written into. A name carrying a `/` is refused: that is a bucket and a prefix written into one field.

prefix.description: The key namespace inside the bucket, so one bucket can hold more than this product's artifacts. Empty puts the key layout at the root.

storage_class.description: The S3 storage class objects are written with. Empty means STANDARD. An archive class cannot take delivery of an artifact and is refused when a tier sends one here.

upload_verification.description: How an upload is proven before the local copy is deleted. Empty means readback, which is the expensive one on purpose: a medium that said nothing must never be the one that gets believed on its own word.

credentials.description: Where the credentials come from. Required on a create and on a candidate preflight. Optional on PUT, where omitting it keeps the credential already configured, which it has to: this contract never reports a medium's credential, not even its kind, so a caller cannot resubmit what it never received.

skip_connection_check.description: Writes this destination without proving it first (issue #636). The service runs the same eight-step check POST /storage-mediums/preflight answers, in front of the write, and refuses with MEDIUM_CONNECTION_NOT_PROVEN when it fails; this is the deliberate opt-out, and a destination written under it is marked connection_unverified until a check passes. The mark is the service's own record of the skip and is never taken from the request. It means nothing on POST /storage-mediums/preflight, which IS the check. Omitted or false checks, which is what every create should do.

ImportStorageCredentialsRequest.description: POST /storage-credentials. Sent once; the caller discards its own copy the moment an id comes back. This is the ONLY place in this contract where S3 credential material appears, in either direction, and it is write-only: no operation anywhere echoes it, returns it or derives anything displayable from it.

access_key_id.description: The access key id. Write-only. It is treated as secret alongside the secret access key rather than as a public identifier, because FR-33 forbids a credential reaching a log in whole or in part.

session_token.description: A session token, for a temporary credential. Optional and empty for the ordinary long-lived key a provider console hands out. Write-only.

ImportStorageCredentialsResponse.description: The reference an import returns, and nothing else. There is deliberately no fingerprint, no masked key and no last-four here, unlike ImportSSHKeyResponse's algorithm and fingerprint: an SSH public key's fingerprint is a safe thing to show a person, and nothing derived from an S3 credential is.

id.description: The opaque reference to carry as credentials.credentials_id on a later medium create or candidate preflight. It names nothing about the manager's host, so it is safe on a request body, in a URL and in a terminal transcript.

StorageMediumUsageBySet.description: One backup set's copies on a storage medium.

placements.description: How many of that set's copies are on this medium.

only_copy_here.description: How many of those are the only confirmed copy of their artifact anywhere. This is the population FR-30's invariant is about, and it is reported separately because it calls for a different sentence: `52 copies live here` is information, and `52 artifacts have their only confirmed copy here` is the reason nothing may be deleted on the strength of a check that failed.

StorageMediumUsageResponse.description: What the journal says is currently on one storage medium, listed rather than only counted. It asks the medium nothing: this is what the deployment RECORDED, and whether the endpoint answers right now is the preflight's question, asked separately. A count with no list is not something an operator can act on, which is why the backup sets are here.

placements.description: How many copies name this medium and have not been recorded as gone. A copy pending deletion is counted with the active ones: it is still a copy on that medium, and removing the declaration under it strands the delete as surely as it strands the read.

backup_sets.description: One entry per backup set with copies here, sorted by id.

ListStorageMediumsResponse.description: Every declared storage destination, in declaration order. An object rather than a bare array, matching every other list in this contract: a top-level array has nowhere to grow a field, and the day this needs a count or a cursor it would be a breaking change.

BackendEnumValue.description: One choice an `enum`-kind field offers: the value that is stored, and the words a surface renders for it.

BackendManifestField.description: One thing an operator is asked for when they configure an instance of this backend: what it is called, what KIND of value it is, and whether it is required. It is a declaration of SHAPE and it never carries a value. In particular a `credential`-kind field says only that a credential is needed here; the material itself reaches the engine as a reference (see StorageMediumCredentialsReference) and has no spelling on this boundary at all, which is what makes serving this catalogue to a browser safe.

id.description: The key this value is stored under, lower_snake_case, and deliberately the same spelling the configuration file already uses for the same fact.

kind.description: What this value IS. The set is closed in Go and a manifest may not add to it, so a client may render a control per kind and treat an unknown one as a version mismatch rather than as free text.

values.description: The closed choice set, for `enum` fields and only for those.

pattern.description: An RE2 the value must match, for `string` fields and only for those. Anchored and safe to hand to a client-side regular expression engine, so a form refuses exactly what the server would refuse.

unset_means.description: What an ACCESSOR resolves this field to when the instance leaves it empty. Emphatically not a default to write into a create request: a default written back is a default frozen into the operator's own file by the next settings save (issue #294). A form renders it as the sentence "leave empty for X" and sends nothing.

BackendProbeStep.description: One step of the verification vocabulary, and whether this backend runs it. A skipped step is a first-class outcome and not a quiet pass, so one that does not run carries the sentence explaining why.

step.description: A step name from the same closed, ordered vocabulary MediumPreflightCheck reports against, so a surface can render one list for "what will be checked" and "what was checked".

reason.description: Present exactly when `run` is false, and forbidden when it is true.

BackendProbe.description: How an instance of this backend is verified: which steps of the closed vocabulary apply to it. It declares no procedure. There is no script, no command and no expression anywhere in a manifest, which is EPIC I's decision and not an omission, and it is the reason this document can be served to a browser without handing out an arbitrary-command surface.

steps.description: One entry per step name, in vocabulary order, always. A manifest that omits, repeats or reorders one is refused at load, so a surface renders a fixed list rather than discovering which steps happened to be declared.

BackendManifest.description: One registered backend, declared as data. A destination is an INSTANCE of one of these, and several instances of one backend is the normal case rather than an edge, which is why a manifest carries a label and a summary for a picker and says nothing about any particular destination.

id.description: The backend's name, lower_snake_case, unique across the registry, and never the reserved instance id. This is what a create request names, and it is the same value the CLI's `medium add --type` takes.

role.description: What this backend IS to this engine, as opposed to how bytes reach it. Closed in Go, and EXTENSIBLE on this wire: a build that registers a backend of a shape this list does not name serves the new value here rather than an existing one, which is an additive change under v1 (see docs/api/contract.md, "Compatibility and deprecation rules"). A client must preserve a role it does not recognise and render it as itself; one that switches on this value needs a branch for the unknown case, and one that drops or rewrites an unfamiliar role reports a destination as something it is not.

configurable.description: Whether an instance of this backend can be authored TODAY. False is a registered backend this build cannot yet store or dial: its shape is real, it is served so it can be found and read, and every layer behind this one refuses it by name. A client renders a false row disabled and never submits it - there is no configure step to run and nothing to create, because the create would be refused. True is the ordinary case, and it is what a client should assume of a build too old to send this field.

UnregisteredBackend.description: A transport this build's storage layer understands but which NO manifest declares, so no instance of it can exist. Reported rather than hidden: hiding it answers an operator worse, because somebody who came looking for SFTP learns nothing from a menu that never mentions it and asks again next month, whereas a row saying the shape is understood and is not registered is a real answer. A client renders these as unselectable; there is nothing to send, since a create request naming one is refused by the registry.

transport.description: How bytes would reach a destination of this shape: a protocol or storage-shape name such as `sftp`. A registered backend does not report its transport, because `role` is the product answer to what a backend is; this schema names one because an unregistered shape has no manifest and so no id to be known by. Today's engine dials these through rclone, which is an implementation fact this contract deliberately does not make a client's business.

ListBackendsResponse.description: GET /backends. Read-only by design, for Validator's reason one step further on: a client-extensible backend catalogue would be an arbitrary-backend surface, and a manifest is the one thing in this product that decides what a destination may be. It carries the naming rules alongside the catalogue so the add-a-destination form validates against the rule the server applies rather than a second copy of it.

backends.description: Every backend this build has a manifest for, in registry order.

instance_id_pattern.description: Anchored regular expression source an instance id must match; safe to pass to a client-side regular expression engine. Served rather than hardcoded in a form for RetentionSchema.tier_name_pattern's reason: the rule comes from the engine's own constant, so a form refuses exactly what a hand-edited configuration file would be refused for.

reserved_instance_id.description: The one instance id no operator may choose. It names the drive this deployment's backups land on, it is written by the first-boot seed as instance zero of the local volume backend, and it is refused on every operator-facing path. A form that offers it and then meets the refusal is a worse experience than one that says so in the field.

MediumFieldValue.description: One manifest-declared value, as a pair. A pair list rather than an object keyed by field id, because no schema in this contract is a map and the generator models additionalProperties as a bool only, so a keyed object would arrive in both languages as an untyped blob. An unset optional field is ABSENT from the list rather than present with an empty value: absent is what a manifest's unset_means resolves at read time, and an empty value written back is a product default frozen into the operator's file by the next save (#294). An EMPTY list is meaningful and is not the same as an absent one - these writes replace the whole declared field set, so empty means "this instance carries no values". The list is sorted by field, so one configuration has one body.

field.description: The manifest field id this value is for.

value.description: The value, as the engine validates it: a bool field is "true" or "false". Never empty.

MediumConfigurationRequest.description: One destination's configuration, in the vocabulary its backend's manifest declares (#669). This is what StorageMediumRequest cannot be: that one enumerates S3's fields, so bucket is required and there is no path, and a local volume - the only destination a fresh install has (#670) - cannot be described in it. credentials stays its own reference object because a credential is not a value: it is checked by a different rule, and a value bag that could hold one is a value bag something eventually puts material into (#665's C1-C5).

backend.description: The manifest id this instance is an instance of. Required when the id is not declared yet, because a destination cannot exist unconfigured (Registry.ValidateInstance refuses an absent required field, core/internal/backend/validate.go:228-233) so there is no record to read it off before the values exist. Refused when it disagrees with a declared instance: that would be a different destination under the same name.

fields.description: Every value this instance carries, keyed by manifest field id.

MediumConfigurationResponse.description: What one destination has configured right now, in its backend's vocabulary. credential_configured is a boolean and never the reference: whether a credential exists is what a form needs - it decides whether the credential pair may be left empty - and it is not material, not a path and not a variable name, which is the most that may be said about it either way (FR-33, #665's C3).

fields.description: Every value this instance carries. An unset optional field is absent.

credential_configured.description: Whether this destination names a credential source at all. Nothing about which, and nothing about what is behind it.

Snapshot.description: One snapshot run: what the incremental engine did on one pass over one backup set's source, and what it proved about the result. This is the record the operator surfaces render for a Kopia run, and its shape is the whole reason EPIC K refuses a single "bytes backed up" figure: entries_scanned, logical_bytes, source_bytes_read, repository_bytes_written and content_reused_bytes are five different measurements of one pass, and collapsing them reports a 100 GB tree deduplicated down to 200 MB of new content as a 100 GB upload. A run is identified by run_id, which exists from the moment the pass starts; snapshot_id is the engine's manifest id and exists only once a manifest was committed, so a failed run has the first and not the second.

run_id.description: This run's own durable id, unique across this deployment's journal.

backup_set_id.description: The source/backup-set id this run belongs to, as every surface in this product prints it.

operation_id.description: The durable operation this run was performed under, empty for a run the daemon's own schedule started. Empty is a real answer and says the schedule did it, not that the attribution was lost.

engine.description: Which machinery produced this run: "artifact" or "kopia". Recorded on the row rather than read from the current configuration, so a set whose engine was changed still reports each run under the engine that actually performed it.

repository_domain.description: The repository security boundary this run's snapshot was stored in.

snapshot_id.description: The engine's opaque manifest id. Absent until a manifest is committed, which is what distinguishes a run that stored something from one that did not.

phase.description: The run's durable phase: SOURCE_SCAN, SNAPSHOT_WRITE, MANIFEST_COMMITTED, VERIFICATION, SUCCESS, FAILED, QUARANTINED, LOST or DELETED. Only SUCCESS is a restore point.

consistency_mode.description: What the operator had arranged around the source while this pass read it: live_best_effort, externally_quiesced or external_snapshot. Recorded per run, because it is a claim about the moment the data was read and not about the configuration as it stands now.

verification_level.description: The level this run was CONFIGURED for, which is what the operator asked for.

verification_level_achieved.description: The level a verification actually PROVED, absent when nothing was proven. Never the same field as verification_level and never filled in from it: a run asking for a full content verification that only managed a structural one has to read as exactly that.

verification_status.description: Whether a verification ran and what it concluded: pending, passed or failed. Absent when none has been attempted.

entries_scanned.description: How many source entries this pass considered, of every kind, including the ones it deliberately skipped. It is not files plus directories: that reconstruction leaves out everything a pass refused. Null is not zero and must never be rendered as zero: it means NOBODY MEASURED THIS, which is the honest state of a run that died before its manifest was recorded and of a snapshot crash reconciliation adopted from the repository.

files.description: Files in the snapshot. Null is not zero and must never be rendered as zero: it means NOBODY MEASURED THIS, which is the honest state of a run that died before its manifest was recorded and of a snapshot crash reconciliation adopted from the repository.

directories.description: Directories in the snapshot. Null is not zero and must never be rendered as zero: it means NOBODY MEASURED THIS, which is the honest state of a run that died before its manifest was recorded and of a snapshot crash reconciliation adopted from the repository.

logical_bytes.description: The size of the tree as the source described it. This is what was SCANNED and is never what was uploaded. Null is not zero and must never be rendered as zero: it means NOBODY MEASURED THIS, which is the honest state of a run that died before its manifest was recorded and of a snapshot crash reconciliation adopted from the repository.

source_bytes_read.description: Bytes this pass actually pulled off the source. An incremental engine still reads the source; this is what that cost. Null is not zero and must never be rendered as zero: it means NOBODY MEASURED THIS, which is the honest state of a run that died before its manifest was recorded and of a snapshot crash reconciliation adopted from the repository.

repository_bytes_written.description: Bytes that actually landed in the repository's storage, after deduplication and compression. The only one of these numbers that is storage growth. Null is not zero and must never be rendered as zero: it means NOBODY MEASURED THIS, which is the honest state of a run that died before its manifest was recorded and of a snapshot crash reconciliation adopted from the repository.

content_reused_bytes.description: Bytes this pass did not have to store again, because the repository already held that content. The gap between read and written. Null is not zero and must never be rendered as zero: it means NOBODY MEASURED THIS, which is the honest state of a run that died before its manifest was recorded and of a snapshot crash reconciliation adopted from the repository.

source_complete.description: The source side's own verdict that the pass covered every entry it was asked to. Null means NOBODY RECORDED A VERDICT, which is what a run that died before its manifest was recorded and a manifest adopted by reconciliation both genuinely are; it is a different claim from "the pass was incomplete", and neither of them is a restore point.

last_known_good.description: Whether this is the one run per backup set whose snapshot may be offered as a restore point.

reason.description: One sentence: why it failed, why it was quarantined, why it is lost. Operator prose, redacted on the way into the journal.

completed_at.description: When the run came to rest. Absent while it is in flight.

duration_seconds.description: How long the run took, in whole seconds. Null while the run is still in flight, because a duration for something that has not finished is a measurement of now rather than of the run.

delete_requested_at.description: The durable intent to delete this snapshot, recorded before the repository was asked for anything. Present on a snapshot retention has decided against and not yet finished removing.

holds.description: Every unreleased hold over this snapshot. A held snapshot is never deleted by retention, whatever the tier chain says.

SnapshotHold.description: One hold: a durable statement that a named snapshot must not be deleted, whoever's retention policy says otherwise, until somebody releases it. A hold is the mechanism an investigation, a legal request or a suspected corruption uses, so it names who placed it and why: a hold nobody can attribute is one nobody dares release.

hold_id.description: This hold's own id, which is what releases it.

run_id.description: The snapshot run this hold protects.

backup_set_id.description: The source/backup-set id that run belongs to.

reason.description: Why the hold was placed, in the words of whoever placed it. Required when a hold is placed: a hold with no reason cannot be safely released by anybody except the person who placed it, and they leave.

placed_by.description: The actor who placed it: an account name, or the surface that placed it on somebody's behalf.

released_at.description: When the hold was released. Absent while the hold is active, which is the same fact as active being true and is reported both ways because a history renders the timestamp and a control renders the boolean.

active.description: Whether this hold still protects the snapshot.

SnapshotTransition.description: One edge of the snapshot state machine, as it actually happened. The run record is overwritten by every advance, so it can say what a run IS and never how it got there: a run verified twice because a crash interrupted the first attempt reads identically on the row to one verified once, and this log is what tells them apart.

from.description: The phase left, empty for the row that created the run.

detail.description: The sentence recorded with the transition, redacted on the way in.

SnapshotResponse.description: GET /backup-sets/{source}/{set}/snapshots/{run}: one run, plus the transition log that says how it got where it is. The log is on the detail read and not on the list because it is unbounded per run and nothing on a list renders it.

ListSnapshotHoldsResponse.description: GET /backup-sets/{source}/{set}/holds: every unreleased hold in this backup set's snapshot lineage.

SnapshotRetentionTier.description: One reason a snapshot survived: which tier selected it, and what about the snapshot the tier selected it for.

tier.description: The tier's name, the protected term a last-known-good snapshot is kept under, or the hold term for one a hold kept.

selected_by.description: The placement inside the tier's bucket that selected this snapshot -- the newest in the day, the newest in the month. Empty for last-known-good protection, which has no placement and whose tier name already says what kind of thing it is; rendering a placement beside it would read as one.

SnapshotRetentionVerdict.description: What snapshot retention would do about one snapshot, and why. Three actions and never two: KEEP means something selects it, DELETE means nothing does and every safety check passed, and REFUSE means it was a delete candidate and something stopped it. Folding REFUSE into KEEP would hide the only one of the three that needs somebody to look at it.

run_id.description: The catalog row this decision is about.

snapshot_id.description: The manifest in the repository, empty for a run that committed none.

started_at.description: When the run that produced this snapshot began, which is the instant the classifier bucketed it by.

tiers.description: Every reason this snapshot survived. Populated only on KEEP.

holds.description: The unreleased holds over this snapshot, whether or not they are what kept it. Naming them is the point: "kept by a hold" is unactionable without knowing which hold and who placed it.

reason.description: The sentence an operator reads: which tier kept it, or that nothing did and every check passed, or exactly what refused it.

hold_reason.description: Set on a REFUSE, and only when the refusal is about the whole backup SET rather than this snapshot: the restore point this set advertises could not be confirmed, or the catalog stopped being able to record what the pass was doing. A separate field rather than something a client matches out of reason, so a wording change is not an alerting change.

SnapshotRetentionResponse.description: GET /backup-sets/{source}/{set}/snapshot-retention: what this set's snapshot retention would decide right now, oldest snapshot first. It is a PREVIEW and changes nothing. This is not /backup-sets/{source}/{set}/retention, and the two must not be confused: that one is FR-18's artifact retention policy, and this one is the per-snapshot verdict the incremental engine's own pruner would reach.

generated_at.description: The instant these verdicts were decided against. Nothing is cached: a retention preview is only true for the moment it names.

RepositoryHealth.description: One repository domain's own health, which is a different question from any backup set's. A set can be perfectly fresh while the repository holding its snapshots is unwritable, out of maintenance, or reachable only by a process whose clock has drifted far enough to mis-order manifests -- and none of those show up in a freshness verdict. Every probe here is reported separately rather than reduced to one boolean, because the remedies are different: unreachable is a mount, unwritable is a permission, invalid credentials is a passphrase, and overdue maintenance is a schedule.

may_share.description: Whether the configuration lets more than one backup set store snapshots in this domain.

state.description: healthy, degraded or failing, using the same vocabulary the backup-set half of this model already uses so one dashboard has one severity scale.

reachable.description: Whether the repository's storage could be contacted at all.

readable.description: Whether this deployment could read the repository's own format metadata. A location that is reachable and unreadable is the shape an empty or wrong mount presents, which is exactly the case that must never be mistaken for "no repository yet".

writable.description: Whether this deployment could write to the repository. Proven by a write this deployment then removes, in the reserved namespace, never by inference from a successful read.

credentials_valid.description: Whether the declared passphrase reference resolves and opens the repository. False with reachable and readable both true is the signature of a rotated or mis-referenced secret.

clock_sane.description: Whether this process's clock agrees with the newest durable timestamp the repository and journal already hold. A clock behind its own history mis-orders manifests and makes retention delete the wrong ones.

clock_skew_seconds.description: How far this process's clock is ahead of (positive) or behind (negative) the newest durable timestamp on record. Null when there is no durable timestamp to compare against, which is a brand-new deployment and not a healthy or unhealthy clock.

maintenance_overdue.description: Whether the repository's own maintenance is past due. Overdue maintenance is not a backup failure and is reported as its own fact: the snapshots are fine and the storage they sit in is growing without being reclaimed.

last_maintenance_at.description: When maintenance last ran to completion. Absent when it never has.

last_maintenance_result.description: What the last maintenance run concluded, empty when none has run.

last_snapshot_at.description: When the newest snapshot in this domain, from any backup set sharing it, came to rest.

last_snapshot_status.description: That snapshot run's durable phase, empty when the domain holds none.

last_verification_at.description: When a verification in this domain last concluded.

last_verification_status.description: What it concluded: passed, failed or pending. Empty when nothing in this domain has ever been verified, which is a real and separate answer from "passed".

backup_sets.description: The source/backup-set ids storing snapshots in this domain. A shared domain's health is every one of their problems.

detail.description: One sentence naming what is wrong, for a domain that is not healthy. Never a path, an endpoint or a credential: this string is rendered on a dashboard and copied into support conversations.

ListRepositoriesResponse.description: GET /repositories: every repository domain this deployment declares, with its health. Nothing is cached, for the reason the backup-set health read is not: a cached repository verdict keeps reporting green after the storage under it has gone away.

RepositoryPassphraseReference.description: Where one repository domain's encryption passphrase comes from: a file on the manager's host, the NAME of an environment variable, or an argv array whose stdout is the secret. Exactly one of the three, and none of them is the passphrase itself. There is deliberately no field to paste one into and there will not be: a repository's passphrase is the only thing standing between its storage and everything this product holds, and a secret that could be typed into a request body is one that ends up in an access log, a terminal transcript and config.yaml in the clear. This is the same three-source shape config.yaml's own repository_domains[].passphrase spells, because "how does a secret reach this process" is one question this product answers once.

file.description: A path on the manager's host to a file whose contents are the passphrase. The preferred source when an operator already provisions secrets as files: what protects it is that file's own mode and owner, and the secret never travels over this API at all.

env.description: The NAME of an environment variable this process reads the passphrase from when it opens the repository. Never a value.

command.description: An argv array whose stdout is the passphrase, run directly and never through a shell. This is how a secrets manager is adopted without this product depending on one.

CreateRepositoryDomainRequest.description: POST /repositories: declare a repository domain. What this persists is a DECLARATION -- an id, a co-tenancy posture and the reference the passphrase is resolved from -- and it creates no store: the repository itself is realized lazily by the first backup run that stores a snapshot in it, exactly as a domain named on the add-backup-set wizard's repository step already is. Nothing here is proven against storage, and nothing here reads it: this route opens no repository and resolves no passphrase reference, so the domain it answers with is described from the declaration alone. Once declared, the domain is probed by GET /repositories, where one nothing has run into yet answers `reachable` true and `readable` false -- the storage answers and holds no repository, which is the truth about it rather than a failure of it.

id.description: How a backup set will name this domain, and the name its maintenance record and its storage are keyed by. Unique across the domains this deployment declares -- a second entry claiming one id is two boundaries with one name, so it is refused with REPOSITORY_DOMAIN_EXISTS rather than merged -- and held to the same rule config.yaml's repository_domains[].id is, which is what refuses a `/` in it.

description.description: The operator's own sentence about what this domain holds. Never interpreted. It is worth sending because a list of five domain ids with no prose is a list nobody reviews, and reviewing it is how an isolation mistake gets caught before an audit does.

isolation.description: Whether more than one backup set may store snapshots here. REQUIRED, with no default in either direction: defaulting to shared would make an isolation boundary a belief rather than a rule, and defaulting to isolated would silently forgo the deduplication that is the reason to run this engine. Sets sharing a domain share its encryption key, its credential, its maintenance owner, its deduplication pool, its corruption blast radius and its disk.
