passphrase.description: Where the passphrase that encrypts this repository comes from. REQUIRED, because a repository this product creates is always encrypted and a domain declared without one is a boundary no backup set can be stored in: config.Validate refuses the set that names it, which is a refusal an operator would meet later, somewhere else, about a different object.

location.description: Where this domain's repository is stored. Empty means this deployment's own storage location, which is the only place this build can put one: a repository domain is a boundary and not a placement, and per-domain storage locations are not in the configuration schema yet. A value naming anywhere else is REFUSED with INVALID_REQUEST rather than accepted and ignored -- a field that silently did nothing is how an operator ends up believing their second copy is off site.

maintenance_owner.description: Which deployment maintains this repository, as a GATE on this one create and nothing more. Empty means `this`. It records nothing: there is no maintenance_owner key in config.yaml and this field is not persisted anywhere, because ADR 0017 makes maintenance ownership a durable record taken by whichever instance first maintains an unclaimed repository and moved afterwards only by transfer -- so a declaration that could name an owner would be exactly the "claim this for me" operation that design exists to make impossible. What the field decides is whether this create is refused as such a claim. `this` is refused with REPOSITORY_DOMAIN_MAINTAINED_ELSEWHERE when a maintenance record for this id already names an owner, which is what a re-declared id or a state directory shared with another instance looks like. `another-instance` says the operator knows that and declares the boundary anyway, and it is the answer that gets the declaration written; which deployment then actually maintains the store is decided by that durable record and by transfer, never by this field.

RepositoryMaintenance.description: GET /repositories/{domain}/maintenance: who owns this repository's maintenance, when it last ran and when it is next eligible. Ownership is the load-bearing part: several deployments may share one repository, exactly one of them may run maintenance on it, and an operator looking at a repository that is not being maintained needs to know whether that is because nobody owns it or because the owner is somebody else.

owner.description: The deployment that currently owns maintenance for this repository, empty when nobody does. Ownership does not lapse on a clock: it moves when an owner hands it over or when another instance claims a repository nobody owns, so there is deliberately no companion field saying when this claim expires.

last_quick_at.description: When a quick maintenance last completed.

last_full_at.description: When a full maintenance last completed. Full maintenance is what actually reclaims storage; a repository with recent quick runs and no full run is growing.

next_eligible_at.description: The earliest instant the next run may start.

due.description: Whether maintenance is due right now.

due_mode.description: Which mode is due: quick or full. Empty when nothing is.

due_reason.description: Why it is or is not due, in one sentence.

overdue.description: Whether the repository has gone long enough without maintenance to be worth an operator's attention, which is a stronger claim than due.

runs.description: How many maintenance runs the retained history records.

reclaimed_bytes.description: How much storage the retained history says maintenance has reclaimed.

failing.description: Whether the most recent run failed. Separate from the failure count, because a repository whose last ten runs failed and one whose first run failed a year ago are different situations.

SnapshotRestoreRequest.description: POST /operations' parameters when the action is restore_snapshot: read a restore point this deployment holds and write a tree onto a disk it can reach. It is a different act from restore_placement and the two are never folded together -- that one asks a storage provider to make an archived object readable again, over hours, at a cost, and writes nothing anywhere.

backup_set_id.description: The source/backup-set id whose restore point is being read.

snapshot_id.description: Which restore point to read, as the engine's manifest id. Omitted means this set's last-known-good snapshot, which is the only snapshot this product advertises as a restore point. It is the MANIFEST id and not a run id on purpose: the catalog is this deployment's account of its own runs, and a restore point the repository holds and the catalog has forgotten -- a journal restored from an older backup, a row a migration lost -- is exactly the situation somebody is restoring in, so the repository decides whether the id names anything.

source_path.description: The path INSIDE the snapshot to restore, relative to the snapshot root, slash separated. Omitted restores the whole tree.

target_path.description: The local directory to restore into, on the machine running this deployment. Required, and never invented: a restore writes somebody's data onto a disk somebody owns, and an engine that chose the disk would fill it.

conflict.description: What happens when the destination already holds something. refuse, the default, stops rather than replacing anything: a restore that silently overwrote a newer local file destroyed the thing somebody was trying to compare against. skip leaves what is there and restores the rest; overwrite replaces it.

SnapshotVerifyRequest.description: POST /operations' parameters when the action is verify_snapshot: prove, now, that a restore point is actually restorable, at a stated depth. It records nothing onto the snapshot row -- what a RUN proved is what that run proved, and an on-demand check months later is a different claim about a different moment, reported on the operation that performed it.

backup_set_id.description: The source/backup-set id whose snapshot is being verified.

run_id.description: Which snapshot run to verify. Omitted means this set's last-known-good snapshot.

level.description: How deep to look: structural, content_sample, content_full or restore_drill. Omitted means the level the backup set is configured for. The four rungs cost four different amounts and prove four different things, which is why this is a parameter and not a fixed depth.

sample_percent.description: How much of the snapshot's file content a content_sample reads, 1 to 100. Omitted means the level the backup set is configured with. A percentage of FILES rather than of bytes, because damage arrives per file and a byte-proportional sample spends its whole budget inside the largest one.

SnapshotHoldRequest.description: POST /operations' parameters when the action is hold_snapshot: stop retention deleting one named snapshot until somebody releases the hold.

backup_set_id.description: The source/backup-set id the snapshot belongs to.

run_id.description: The snapshot run to hold. Absent means this backup set's last known good snapshot, which is the one an operator protecting "the current restore point" means and the one they would otherwise have to look up first. Both the service layer and `retnd snapshot hold` already read an unnamed run that way, so this is optional rather than required.

reason.description: Why. Required, because a hold with no reason is one nobody except the person who placed it dares release, and they leave.

SnapshotHoldReleaseRequest.description: POST /operations' parameters when the action is release_snapshot_hold: end one hold, by its id. Releasing does not delete anything; it returns the snapshot to whatever the retention policy already said about it.

backup_set_id.description: The source/backup-set id the hold's snapshot belongs to.

hold_id.description: The hold to release, as GET /backup-sets/{source}/{set}/holds reports it.

WorkflowSecretReference.description: Where a workflow environment variable's value comes from, when it is not a literal. It is a LOCATION and never a value, on every surface and in both directions: exactly one of the three is set, and there is no field here -- and deliberately no field anywhere on this contract -- that a resolved secret could be written into or read out of. The engine resolves a reference at the moment a hook is about to run and nothing carries the result back. The consequence is worth stating because it looks like a gap: no read on this API can show an operator the value of a secret variable, ever. It shows the name and where the value comes from, because a surface that could print it would be a surface an attacker holding one session could read every credential in the deployment from. It is the same file/env/command triple a repository passphrase and a storage destination's credentials already use, spelled the same way.

file.description: A path on the deployment's own host whose contents are the value. The path, never the contents.

env.description: The NAME of an environment variable in the engine's own process, never its value.

command.description: A program and its arguments, executed by the engine to print the value, as an argv rather than a shell string so nothing re-splits it. It is the caller's own words, so a client that renders this as a runnable command line is rendering something that may itself be a credential (`printf %s hunter2` is a valid secret command): `retnd` prints the flag with a placeholder and never the words.

WorkflowEnvironmentVariable.description: One configured workflow environment entry, as every read of either scope reports it.

name.description: The variable name a hook will see. Held to the engine's own name rule, which refuses this product's reserved RETND_ prefix, and its deprecated BACKUPD_ spelling for as long as the runtime still exports that too: a hook cannot be given a variable that would shadow the run facts the engine injects.

value.description: The literal, when this variable has one. A literal is the operator's own plain text as it stands in config.yaml and is not a secret reference, so it is reported as configured; a variable whose value comes from a secret reference has no literal here and never will (see WorkflowSecretReference). Empty on its own does not mean "no literal": read has_value beside it.

has_value.description: Whether a literal is configured at all, which is what tells a deliberately empty variable (`value: ""`, which operators write on purpose) apart from a variable with no literal. Two fields rather than a nullable one because the wire shape is read by a UI that has to render the difference, and "absent" and "empty string" are different configurations.

secret.description: Where the value comes from when it is not a literal. Every field empty means this variable is a literal.

ListWorkflowEnvironmentResponse.description: One scope's configured workflow environment, after a read or a write. The write operations answer with the whole list rather than with the one entry they touched, because a set/unset is only meaningful against what else is there: an operator clearing a credential needs to see what is left, and the entry they just wrote is in the answer either way.

backup_set_id.description: Which scope this list belongs to, as a source/backup-set id. Empty means the deployment-wide layer, which is the layer every backup set inherits from; one field rather than two routes' worth of separate shapes, because the two are the same list at two levels and a second shape would be a second place the secret-reference rule has to be kept.

variables.description: The entries configured at this scope, sorted by name. Sorted because this list is re-marshalled into config.yaml on every save, and an operator diffing two revisions of that file should see their own change rather than a reordering.

WorkflowEnvironmentVariableRequest.description: PUT one workflow environment entry, at the deployment scope or at one backup set's. The variable's NAME is the last path segment and is deliberately not a field here: a body that could name a second variable would be a request whose path and body can disagree, and the engine would then have to decide which one the operator meant. Exactly one of `value` and one spelling of `secret` must be present. A write REPLACES the entry of that name rather than merging with it, because a merge would make "change this from a literal to a secret" inexpressible: the literal would survive beside the reference, which the configuration validator then refuses as a contradiction.

value.description: The literal to configure. Present with an empty string is a deliberately empty variable, which is a real configuration an operator writes; absent means this variable's value comes from `secret` instead. The two are different requests, which is why this field is nullable rather than a plain string.

secret.description: Where the engine should read the value from at hook time. Every field empty means no secret reference was named, in which case `value` must be.

WorkflowRunnerSettings.description: How THIS PROCESS reaches the Host Workflow Runner, the component that executes a `.local.sh` hook on the machine retnd is installed on. Reported and not writable here: the two paths differ between a container and a bare-metal install of the same deployment, so they are a deployment-shape fact the installer writes rather than a policy an operator tunes, exactly like the SSH key, the known_hosts file and the state database.

configured.description: Whether this process has a runner socket to talk to at all. False means a local hook cannot run here, which is a deployment that was installed without the runner rather than a deployment that has none configured.

socket.description: The Unix socket path this process will connect to.

token_file.description: The path this process reads the runner's shared token from. A path, never the token.

WorkflowSettingsResponse.description: The deployment-wide workflow configuration, RESOLVED: the timeout a hook will actually get, the stages that will actually run, the environment a hook will actually see. That is why this read exists rather than a client re-reading config.yaml: the file's whole point is that it omits what is inherited or defaulted, so a re-serialization of it cannot answer what a run will do.

configured.description: Whether this deployment runs workflows at all, which is exactly "is a workflow root set". A deployment with no root has no approved tree for hook scripts to live in, so every per-set workflow write is refused until one is.

root.description: The one directory hook scripts may live under. Every stage directory is resolved inside it and a path that escapes it is refused, which is the containment the whole feature rests on: a hook is arbitrary code, and the root is the operator's statement of where code they approved lives.

before_dir.description: The deployment-wide "before" stage directory, relative to the root. Empty disables that stage.

after_dir.description: The deployment-wide "after" stage directory, relative to the root. Empty disables that stage.

script_timeout_seconds.description: The bound one hook gets when its backup set does not pin one of its own. RESOLVED: a deployment that configures none reports the engine's own default rather than a zero an operator would read as "no bound". Read script_timeout_configured beside it to tell the two apart.

script_timeout_configured.description: Whether the resolved bound above came from the file rather than from the default, which is the difference between "we chose five minutes" and "nobody has chosen".

max_script_size_bytes.description: The largest hook script this deployment will capture and execute. It bounds the spool a run keeps for its own recovery, which is why it is a deployment setting rather than a per-set one.

environment.description: The deployment-wide environment layer, which every backup set's hooks inherit and any set may override by name.

exec_connections.description: The names of the declared remote execution connections a backup set's remote_exec_connection_ref may point at. NAMES ONLY: each declaration carries a whole remote, credentials included, and this is a read surface.

runner.description: The host runner this process will try to reach for a local hook.

UpdateWorkflowSettingsRequest.description: PATCH the deployment-wide workflow block. Every field is nullable because this is a PATCH: "the caller did not mention this" and "the caller wants this cleared" are different requests, and a plain string can only say one of them. Clearing a stage directory is a real operation -- it disables that stage -- so it has to be expressible. A body that names nothing at all is refused rather than answered 200 for a write that changed nothing.

root.description: The approved tree hook scripts must live under. Setting it is what makes this deployment one that runs workflows.

before_dir.description: The deployment-wide "before" stage directory, relative to the root. An empty string clears it, which disables that stage.

after_dir.description: The deployment-wide "after" stage directory, relative to the root. An empty string clears it, which disables that stage.

script_timeout_seconds.description: The default bound for one hook. Zero clears the deployment's own bound, after which hooks fall back to the engine's default; a negative value is refused by the configuration validator rather than here, so there is no second copy of that rule on this boundary.

max_script_size_bytes.description: The largest hook script this deployment will capture. Zero clears it back to the engine's own bound.

WorkflowStage.description: One scope-and-phase pair that has a directory. A run executes five stages in a fixed order, and these are the ones this configuration actually gives a directory to.

scope.description: Whose hooks these are. It is durable rather than cosmetic: a deployment-wide "after" hook and a per-set "after" hook are two different operator decisions that may both name a script the same thing, and the scope is what keeps them apart in a plan, in a spool path and in an audit.

phase.description: Which side of the backup these hooks run on.

dir.description: The directory, as configured, resolved inside the workflow root.

BackupSetWorkflowResponse.description: One backup set's workflow configuration, resolved against the deployment's. Both halves of every inherited value are reported -- what this set pins and what a hook will actually get -- because an operator changing the deployment default needs to know which sets are pinned and which will follow.

backup_set_id.description: The set this describes, as its source/backup-set id.

configured.description: Whether this set has a workflow block of its own. A set that says nothing still runs the deployment's hooks, which is why this is not the same question as "does this set run hooks": read `stages` for that.

before_dir.description: This set's own "before" stage directory. Empty means it declares none, not that none runs: the deployment's may still.

script_timeout_seconds.description: This set's OWN bound, and zero means it inherits. Reported beside the effective value below rather than instead of it, because a set pinning thirty seconds while the deployment allows five minutes is a hook that will be killed, and the only place that is visible is a read that says which value won.

effective_script_timeout_seconds.description: What a hook of this set will actually get, after inheritance and the engine's own default.

remote_exec_connection_ref.description: The declared remote execution connection this set's `.remote.sh` hooks run over, by name. Empty means this set has none, in which case a remote hook cannot run and validation says so rather than the run finding out. The wire spells it as config.yaml's own key so an operator greps for one word; `retnd` spells the same thing --exec-connection.

environment.description: This set's OWN environment entries, which win over the deployment's layer by name.

resolved_environment_names.description: Every variable a hook of this set will have, sorted, NAMES ONLY. Names only for the standing reason this API never carries a resolved secret, and it is not a limitation here: the question this answers is which of an operator's variables win, and a name answers it.

stages.description: The hook directories this set will actually run, in execution order, resolved from the deployment's configuration and this set's. An empty list is a set that runs no hooks at all.

UpdateBackupSetWorkflowRequest.description: PATCH one backup set's workflow block. Every field is nullable for the reason the deployment-wide patch's are: an absent field and a cleared one are different requests. A patch against a set that has no workflow block creates one, carrying only the fields the request named -- so a set given a before_dir does not silently acquire a pinned timeout copied from today's deployment value, which would make it stop following a later change to that value.

before_dir.description: This set's "before" stage directory, relative to the workflow root. An empty string clears it.

after_dir.description: This set's "after" stage directory, relative to the workflow root. An empty string clears it.

script_timeout_seconds.description: The bound this set pins for its own hooks. Zero clears the pin, after which the set follows the deployment's value again.

remote_exec_connection_ref.description: The declared remote execution connection this set's remote hooks run over, by name. An empty string clears it, which leaves the set unable to run a remote hook.

WorkflowFinding.description: One validation check's answer about one backup set's hooks.

check.description: Which check this is, from a closed vocabulary rather than free text: a client that groups by check, or an operator who greps for one, needs the id to be a value. The SENTENCE is `detail` and is free to be rewritten; this is not.

severity.description: How bad it is. `skipped` is the one that earns its place: a deployment with no remote hooks has nothing to say about its remote exec capability, and reporting that as `ok` would be this product claiming it proved something it never looked at.

detail.description: The operator-facing sentence. It may name a script by basename, a stage directory as configured, a variable NAME and a secret's LOCATION -- and never a secret's value, because nothing on the path that produces it resolves one.

scope.description: Which scope's hook this finding is about, empty for a finding about the set as a whole.

phase.description: Which phase's hook this finding is about, empty for a finding about the set as a whole.

target.description: Where the hook this finding is about would run, empty for a finding about the set as a whole.

script.description: The script this finding is about, by BASENAME, empty for a finding about the set as a whole.

WorkflowSourceLine.description: One line of a hook script, as an editor would number it. The text arrives with control characters removed and its length bounded, at the point it is produced rather than at each surface that draws it: a hook is arbitrary text and this text reaches a browser and a terminal.

number.description: The 1-based line number, so it is the number in the gutter of whatever the operator opens the file with.

text.description: The line itself, inert. A tab is rendered as one space rather than dropped, so the reported column still points at the same character.

truncated.description: Whether the line was longer than an excerpt carries, so a reader can tell the script from what they are being shown.

WorkflowSourceExcerpt.description: A few of a hook script's own lines, carried beside a position that names one of them: the reported line with one line either side. It exists because a position on its own is a lookup somebody has to perform on a machine they may not be on -- "BSH003 at 24:10" sends an operator to a NAS over SSH to read one line. The lines come from the bytes this validation READ AND HASHED rather than from a later re-read, so they cannot disagree with the position beside them. They are the script's own text and never a resolved secret: nothing on the path that produces them resolves one.

lines.description: The lines, in order, or empty when the position names no line of this script.

WorkflowLintFinding.description: One thing backupd's own shell rules reported about one hook script. These are this product's own checks, carrying its own BSH codes, and they are NOT ShellCheck: ShellCheck is GPL-3.0 and this product is Apache-2.0, so the analysis is implemented here against a Go shell parser's syntax tree rather than shipped as somebody else's tool. The set is deliberately small and conservative; an operator who wants a general shell linter should run one.

code.description: Which rule this is, e.g. BSH003, from a closed vocabulary rather than free text: a client that groups by it, or an operator who greps for one, needs the id to be a value. The MESSAGE is free to be reworded and this is not.

severity.description: How bad it is, and it decides one thing besides colour: `error` refuses a workflow SAVE, the other three are reported and saved. That threshold is documented rather than tunable, because a gate that refused a warning would be a gate operators work around by not using this product's configuration surfaces.

line.description: The 1-based line the finding is about. This position is the whole value of this check over `bash -n` through a runner, which could only ever report that a script did not parse.

col.description: The 1-based column, counted the way an editor counts.

message.description: The rule's sentence: what is wrong, what it does when it goes wrong, and what to write instead. It may quote a variable NAME or a literal from the script -- the script's own text -- and never a resolved secret, because nothing on the path that produces it resolves one.

WorkflowScriptLint.description: What backupd's own shell verification established about one hook script's exact bytes, without running any of them. Three states, kept distinguishable on purpose: examined and parsed, examined and refused (a parse error with its position), and NOT EXAMINED, which is a script larger than the verification reads. A client that folded the third into either of the others would report either a pass nobody proved or a fault nobody found.

examined.description: Whether the bytes were read and checked at all.

not_examined_reason.description: Why they were not, and it is never empty when `examined` is false: "not examined" without a reason is the finding an operator cannot act on. Render it as "not examined" and never as a pass.

parsed.description: Whether the bytes are a shell program. The verdict comes from a shell parser linked into this product rather than from a `bash -n` on the far side of a socket or an SSH connection, which is what lets it be a precondition of saving on a deployment whose runner is unreachable.

parse_error.description: The parser's own message, empty when the script parses.

parse_error_line.description: The 1-based line the parser stopped at, 0 when the script parses.

parse_error_col.description: The 1-based column the parser stopped at, 0 when the script parses.

findings.description: Every finding, in position order, at every severity -- including the ones that do not block a save. A client that was only given the blocking ones could not show an operator the warning they are about to introduce.

WorkflowValidatedScript.description: One hook this backup set would run, as validation found it on disk, with what retnd's own shell verification established about its bytes. Nothing here was executed: the syntax verdict and the findings come from parsing and walking the bytes in this process, and the only things validation ever hands an interpreter are `bash -n`, which parses and never runs, and this product's own fixed remote capability probe.

step_id.description: The id this script's step would carry in a run, which is what makes a finding and a later run row line up.

order.description: Its position in the plan. The plan is ordered bytewise by name within a stage, so the order is reproducible rather than filesystem-dependent.

script_name.description: The script's basename, which is also where its target comes from: a target that were configurable would mean the same bytes could be moved and then run somewhere else, so it is a property of the filename and is mandatory.

phase.description: Which side of the backup it runs on.

target.description: Where it runs: on the machine this daemon is installed on, or on the host the backup set pulls from.

sha256.description: The hash of the bytes as they are on disk right now. It is what a run would record and what a recovery would re-verify against, so two deployments meant to be configured alike can be compared on it.

size_bytes.description: The script's size in bytes, which is what the deployment's max_script_size_bytes bounds.

timeout_ms.description: The resolved bound this script would get, in milliseconds. Milliseconds because this is the value the engine will actually enforce, and a 300ms bound rendered as "0 seconds" would be a lie; the CONFIGURED policy it is derived from is reported in seconds, which is the unit an operator sets.

execution_connection_ref.description: The connection a remote script would run over, empty for a local one.

WorkflowValidationResponse.description: Everything this product can establish about one backup set's hooks WITHOUT running any of them. Two verdicts rather than one, and that is the shape rather than an oversight: a backup set whose source connects, whose destination is writable and whose retention is sound, with a hook directory somebody has not created yet, is valid for backup and invalid for workflows -- which is the normal case during setup, and reporting it as a broken backup set would tell an operator their backups are failing when they are not.

backup_set_id.description: The set this report is about.

valid_for_backup.description: Whether anything is wrong with the backup set ITSELF.

workflow_valid.description: Whether anything is wrong with its hooks. A set with no stages reports true with every check skipped, which is the honest answer: there is nothing to be wrong.

configured.description: Whether this set runs hooks at all.

root.description: The approved tree the stages below were resolved inside.

stages.description: The stages this set would run, in execution order.

scripts.description: Every hook this set would run, in plan order.

findings.description: One entry per check, sorted into check order so two runs of this read over an unchanged deployment produce identical output: a report an operator cannot diff is one they cannot use to find out what they just changed.

WorkflowStep.description: One step of one workflow run: one hook script, executed once.

step_id.description: The step's own id, stable for the life of the run. It is what a log read is scoped to.

order.description: The step's position in the plan it came from.

phase.description: Which side of the backup it ran on.

execution_connection_ref.description: The connection a remote step ran over, empty for a local one.

state.description: What became of this step. A step holds one of the EIGHT step states and never one of the four a RUN adds (recovery_required, cleanup_running, cleanup_failed, recovered): those describe what became of a run as a whole, and internal/workflow's StepStates() is the vocabulary this field is validated against.

exit_code.description: The process's exit status, and null unless a process exited and this product OBSERVED the status. Null and 0 are not the same answer, which is this feature's standing rule: transport loss is never reported as a known exit code, because "the hook said it was fine" and "we never found out" are the two answers an operator most needs to tell apart.

termination_confirmed.description: Whether this product PROVED the process was gone after asking it to stop. False on a step that ended by itself, and the field matters on the ones that did not: a timed-out hook whose termination was never confirmed may still be holding whatever it was holding.

timeout_ms.description: The bound this step was run under, in milliseconds. See WorkflowValidatedScript.timeout_ms for why run-time facts are milliseconds here and configured policy is seconds.

started_at.description: When this step began, empty for a step that never started.

finished_at.description: When it ended, empty while it is still running or if it never started.

duration_ms.description: How long it took, or how long it has been running when finished_at is empty.

WorkflowRun.description: One workflow run: one backup set's pass, wrapped in the five-stage hook lifecycle. The three statuses stay three, and none of them is derived from the others. That is the whole reason the journal has three columns: "the backup succeeded and the cleanup did not" is the single most operationally important thing this feature can report -- it means a machine may be sitting quiesced with a good backup beside it -- and any surface that collapsed the three into one verdict would make exactly that case unsayable.

run_id.description: The run's own id, which every other workflow read is addressed by.

backup_set_id.description: The backup set this run belongs to.

backup_status.description: What happened to the BACKUP. `unknown` is a real value rather than an absence: it is the honest answer while the backup has not run, and an unset field and a field saying "nobody knows yet" read identically to a client that treats empty as false.

cleanup_status.description: What happened to the "after" hooks, which is a separate fact from the backup's outcome in both directions.

workflow_status.description: What happened to the workflow as a whole.

recovery_state.description: Whether this run is blocking its backup set. `required` means an interruption nobody has dealt with, and the set will refuse to run until somebody resumes the cleanup or acknowledges it by hand.

bypassed.description: Whether this run's hooks were deliberately skipped. Recorded durably on the row, so "the hooks stopped running some time last month" is a question with an answer.

failed_step.description: The step that broke the run -- the FIRST one, because everything after it is a consequence -- and empty for a run that did not fail.

failed_script.description: That step's script, by BASENAME rather than by path, because this value also reaches a notification that leaves the deployment.

finished_at.description: When it ended, empty while it is still running.

duration_ms.description: How long the run took, or how long it has been running when finished_at is empty.

script_count.description: How many hook scripts the plan declared. Zero is a run of a set with no hooks, which still exists as a row because the recovery check is asked of every run.

steps.description: Every step in plan order. It is EMPTY on a list read and populated on a detail read: a list of thirty runs each carrying its steps is thirty journal queries for a page nobody reads the steps from.

ListWorkflowRunsResponse.description: A page of workflow runs, newest first.

runs.description: The runs, each without its steps. Read one run, or its steps, to get those.

ListWorkflowStepsResponse.description: One run's steps, in plan order. Its own operation rather than a field on the run detail because a client following a running workflow polls the steps and not the run: the run's own row moves once at the start and once at the end, and the steps are what change in between.

run_id.description: The run these steps belong to, echoed so a client holding a page has the identity beside it.

steps.description: Every step of the run, in plan order.

WorkflowStepLogRecord.description: One captured record of one step's output.

seq.description: The run-monotonic cursor. It never repeats within a run and never starts at zero, so a follower's "everything after N" is exact. It is per RUN and not per step, which is why a page filtered to one step can be empty while the counter has moved.

stream.description: Which of the hook's two output streams this came from. They are kept apart end to end: a hook that writes progress to one and errors to the other is telling an operator something, and a merged log throws it away.

kind.description: Whether this record carries the hook's own output or this product's truncation marker. A client that rendered the marker as though the hook had printed it would be attributing this product's sentence to somebody's script.

text.description: The payload, already redacted. Every value resolved from a secret reference for the step that produced it was layered onto the deployment's redactor before a byte of this was written down, and the redaction is STREAMING, so a credential straddling two reads off the pipe is still caught.

WorkflowStepLogPage.description: One page of one step's captured output. It is a cursor read and not a stream, and that decision is about where this product runs: a held-open response is at the mercy of every buffering proxy and idle timeout between here and the client, and a design that only works when nothing in the path buffers is not a design. The follower sends the last sequence it PROCESSED and gets what is newer, so resume after a dropped connection is not a special case at all -- it is the ordinary read, with the cursor the follower already had. Each page is one ordinary authenticated request, which is also what makes authorization on replay structural rather than something somebody has to remember.

run_id.description: The run this page belongs to.

step_id.description: The step this page is scoped to. A log read names one run AND one step; there is no read of a whole run's interleaved output, because a follower of one hook must not have to filter somebody else's.

records.description: The records above the caller's cursor, oldest first, bounded by the limit.

cursor.description: The sequence to send as `after` next time: the last record in this page, or the caller's own `after` when the page is empty. Echoed rather than left to the client to compute, so an empty page does not make a follower forget where it was. It advances past records belonging to OTHER steps of the same run, which is why it can move while this page is empty -- a follower that only advanced past its own step's records would re-read the same window forever on a run whose later steps are noisy.

truncated.description: Whether this step's recording stopped at the persisted-output bound at some point up to the cursor. It is a property of the LOG rather than of this page, so it stays true on every page after the marker: a follower that joined late must still be told the record is incomplete.

complete.description: Whether the step has finished AND this page reached the end of its output, so a follower may stop. It is the only thing that distinguishes "nothing new yet" from "there will never be anything new", and without it a follow of a finished step never exits.

step_state.description: The step's state at the moment the page was read, which is what a client renders beside the tail. The eight STEP states, for WorkflowStep.state's reason: this is the state of the step whose output this page carries, so a run-only state could never appear here.

WorkflowRecoveryHold.description: One reason a backup set is refusing to run: a workflow run whose cleanup this product could not finish, and whose "after" hooks may therefore never have run.

run_id.description: The run holding the set. It is what a resume or an acknowledgement is addressed to.

backup_set_id.description: The set that will refuse to run until this is settled.

scope.description: Which nesting level's cleanup is outstanding: the deployment's own hooks, or this backup set's.

entered_at.description: When that scope was entered, which is the answer to the first question an operator asks: how long has this machine been left like this.

spool_ref.description: The run's retained copy of the scripts a resume would execute. It is reported deliberately: an operator deciding between resuming and acknowledging wants to read the hooks first, and this is where they are. It is a path this product created under its own state directory, not a credential.

WorkflowRecoveryResponse.description: Every outstanding recovery hold in this deployment, sorted. An empty list is a deployment where no backup set is being held, which is the ordinary state.

holds.description: The holds, one per outstanding cleanup scope.

WorkflowAcknowledgementRequest.description: Take responsibility, by hand, for a workflow run this product could not account for, and unblock its backup set. There is deliberately no "clear this" and no "ignore this": a run in recovery may have left a source machine quiesced, mounted or paused right now, so the only two honest exits are to RUN the cleanup that is owed (resume-cleanup) or for a person to state, in words that are recorded, that they have dealt with it themselves.

reason.description: What the operator did, or why it does not matter. REQUIRED and refused when blank, because the whole value of the record is answering, six months later, why a backup set was unblocked without its cleanup ever running -- and an acknowledgement with no reason is a button somebody presses to make a warning go away, which is precisely the outcome the recovery axis exists to prevent.

The second is its own code rather than an invalid request because the request is well formed and the set is the wrong kind: an artifact set has no snapshots to restore, verify or hold, and a client reading a generic validation failure would offer the operator a fix to the body.

409.description: Refused: CONFIG_REVISION_STALE, IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_CONFLICT, OPERATION_ALREADY_RUNNING, BACKUP_SET_HELD_FOR_EDITING, RESTORE_REFUSED, SNAPSHOT_NOT_HOLDABLE. SNAPSHOT_NOT_HOLDABLE is the state of the snapshot rather than of the request: the run committed no manifest, or its snapshot is already gone, already being deleted, or not in the repository at all, so a hold accepted now would protect nothing. It is distinct from BACKUP_SET_NOT_INCREMENTAL, which is about the SET being the wrong kind: this one is answered by enabling incremental_engine.enabled in the deployment's configuration (or RETND_INCREMENTAL_ENGINE=1 in the engine process's environment), never by changing the request. get.summary: One page of one step's captured output, from a cursor, optionally waiting briefly for more. Read-only and scoped to one run and one step. It is a cursor poll rather than an event stream for the reason GET /activity/live is: a held-open response has to survive every buffering proxy and idle timeout an operator already had in front of their NAS, and a design that only works when nothing in the path buffers is not a design. That choice has a security consequence worth stating, because it is the reason this route needs no authorization machinery of its own: every page, INCLUDING every resume after a dropped connection, is one ordinary authenticated request, so a session that has since expired or been signed out is refused on the next page. A long-lived stream is the shape that makes replay-time authorization a separate thing somebody has to remember.

parameters.name: step
parameters.description: The step's id, within that run. A log read is scoped to both, because the sequence counter is per run and a page filtered to one step is the only read a follower of one hook can use.

parameters.name: after
parameters.description: The last sequence the caller PROCESSED. Only records above it come back. Omitted, zero or unparseable reads from the beginning, which is the historical read: a sequence never starts at zero, so no such value can name a position, and re-reading from the start is the only honest answer to a cursor that names none. The subscriber owns its cursor because only the subscriber knows what it handled, which is what makes resume after a drop the ordinary read rather than a special case.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: How many records to return. Omitted, unparseable or non-positive means the engine's default; above its maximum is clamped rather than refused.

parameters.name: wait
parameters.description: How many seconds to wait for output newer than `after` before answering with what there is. Omitted, unparseable or non-positive never blocks. It exists so that tailing a hook which prints a line every thirty seconds is not a poll loop choosing between latency and load, and it is BOUNDED and clamped to the engine's ceiling: an unbounded wait is a held-open response wearing a different name. The wait is served from the engine's own non-blocking fan-out and can never slow a hook down.
